## [PDF page 66]
From Territorial Security to Societal Security  31
Ultimately, we want to enhance human safety to achieve societal  
resilience. Our society should be able to withstand an attack, mute its  
effects, and recover from the assault. These objectives should inform  
security priorities.
I posit that societal security should be composed of two elements:  
cohesion and physical protection. In this context, cohesion refers to  
the values and qualities that bind a community together which are rel-  
evant to security, which are: democracy, the rule of law and civil liber-  
ties, education, welfare, and pluralism. Our security policies must not  
degrade these features, which are central to what makes our society  
worth defending in the first place.
Democracy is a fundamental component of creating a just society  
providing a mechanism for the governed to select their leaders and  
participate in decision-making. A just society is better and more stable  
than an unjust one (although the transition to democracy can be  
destabilizing). The rule of law and civil liberty promote and protect  
equality and liberty and create the political climate of trust necessary  
for the connections of modern life to thrive. Education and adequate  
economic well-being are crucial for the human spirit to flourish. Lack  
of access to education and social exclusion or degradation undermine  
cohesion. Pluralism is particularly important, but not well understood.  
Pluralism defends a diversity of cultural and religious expressions  
within a framework of tolerance guided by certain rules. Pluralism  
requires that all accept certain principles, including respect for  
others. Unlike multiculturalism, which tends to confine people in sep-  
arate cultural traditions, the concept of pluralism better allows each  
person to fulfill complex multiple identities while maintaining overall  
cohesion.
The elements of physical protection include infrastructure, public  
health, natural disaster relief, environmental quality and anti-terror-  
ism measures aimed at thwarting attacks within the U.S. In my socie-  
tal security model, fighting terrorism is portrayed as a crosscutting  
policy, not a fundamental sphere of security. Fighting terrorism is an  
important policy action, but it should not be the defining framework  
for our strategic outlook.
We can draw on several theoretical traditions to understand how to  
arrange priorities within the concept of societal security. Our efforts

## [PDF page 67]
32  Transforming Homeland Security
to enhance human safety can benefit from a rich theoretical tradition  
that endeavors to highlight the role of the individual person in inter-  
national affairs. In this section I will draw from four traditions: com-  
mon security, human needs, human security and Nordic notions of  
societal security. The first three emerge from policy debates within  
the economic development community. From their efforts to define  
the good society and hence the ultimate goal of development, devel-  
opment experts honed useful concepts about ways to enhance human  
well-being that can help us understand which themes are most  
important when developing our notion of human safety within socie-  
tal security.
In the latter portion of the Cold War, there were significant efforts  
to recover notions of human value amid the overwhelming concern  
with state security and the threat of nuclear war between the super-  
powers. In their reports North-South: A Program for Survival  (1980)  
and  Common Crisis: North-South Cooperation for World Recovery  (1983),  
the Independent Commission on International Development Issues  
led by former German chancellor Willy Brandt sought to connect  
development issues and strategic world order concerns. The Brandt  
Commission discussed the interplay between social issues that directly  
affect people such as hunger, poverty, and human rights with interna-  
tional economic and security affairs. The related notion of common  
security derives from a celebrated international report of the same  
name issued by the Independent Commission on Disarmament and  
Security Issues in 1982. This commission led by Swedish Prime  
Minister Olaf Palme stressed that both East and West had a common  
interest in safety and that security had to be achieved together.9  Taken  
together these well-publicized reports by political leaders raised the  
idea that security needed to include the well-being of people.
The notion that national policies needed to connect to people’ s  
well-being was advanced further by the concept of “basic needs.”

## [PDF page 67]
9  See Independent Commission on International Development Issues, North-South: A  
Program for Survival,  (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1980); The Brandt Commission,  
Common Crisis: North-South Cooperation for World Recovery, (London: Pan Books, 1983);  
and Independent Commission on Disarmament and Security Issues, Common Security: A  
Programme for Disarmament,  (London: Pan Books, 1982); and Andrew Butfoy, “Changing  
Western Conceptions of Global Security,” New Security Agendas, I, available at  
http://www.arts.monash.edu.au/ncas/teach/unit/pol/chpt05.html

## [PDF page 68]
From Territorial Security to Societal Security  33
Again, ferment within the development community produced an idea  
that economic development needed to be geared towards the funda-  
mental elements that sustained human life, not just towards large  
infrastructure projects. Thus, reducing poverty and hunger or increas-  
ing literacy were just (or even more) valid measures than the number  
of highways or bridges built. If economic development can be linked  
to human well-being, then the notion that security can be connected  
to human safety is not a big step.
The third framework discussed here, human security, endeavors to  
make a direct connection between personal safety and national secu-  
rity. Concepts of human security can help us prioritize what features  
must be maintained for human well-being. Human security endeavors  
to use the person rather the state as the unit to be safeguarded, but it  
also acknowledges that people need social constructs for well-being  
(provision of food, maintenance of health, etc.).
There have been several efforts to define human security. Indeed,  
the idea suffers from significant theoretical imprecision.10  However,  
within the more coherent expressions of the idea certain core notions  
can be discerned. The concept of human security appears in a 1994  
report by the United Nations Development Program (UNDP).  
Scholars such as Gary King and Christopher Murray tried to analyze  
the idea more deeply. Meanwhile, the Canadian and other govern-  
ments tried to translate the theory into policy. There was even a  
report on human security by a distinguished international panel  
headed by the former UN High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako  
Ogata and Nobel laureate Amartya Sen.11  Each analysis has a some-  
what different definition. Table 1 lists definitions of human security  
according to the UNDP, King and Murray, and my definition.
10  Roland Paris, “Human Security: Paradigm Shift or Hot Air,” International Security  26 (Fall  
2001): p. 99.

## [PDF page 68]
11  See United Nations Development Program, Human Development Report  (New York:  
Oxford University Press, 1994), pp. 22-38; Gary King and Christopher Murray,  
“Rethinking Human Security,” Harvard University, May 4, 2000,accessed at http://gking.  
harvard.edu/files/hs.pdf; Canadian Department of Foreign Affairs and International  
Trade, www.dfait-maeci.gc.ca/foreignp/humansecurity/menu-e.asp and Commission on  
Human Security. Human Security Now: Protecting and Empowering People  (New York:  
Commission on Human Security, 2003). Available at www.humansecurity-chs.org

Chunks: 0,1,2,3,9,10,11,12,25,26,27,28
Highlights of the interview were broadcast on CNN’s _Fareed Zakaria GPS_ on Sunday, September 27 at 10:00 a.m. (EDT), with a planned replay at 1:00 p.m. (EDT).
ZAKARIA: All right. I’d like to welcome all of you. We have, of course, very distinguished guests with us today—the Prime Minister of Norway, the president of Finland.
This is called the Russell Leffingwell Lecture. And we do want to thank the Leffingwell family for their generosity in endowing this lecture, especially Tom and Ted Leffingwell Pulling. Appreciate it greatly. Russell Leffingwell was a charter member of the CFR who also served as its president from 1944 to ’46, and its chairman from ’46 to ’53.
You know the usual rules for the Council apply. We will begin with a conversation, and then about halfway through I’ll open it up to questions.
Welcome—I can’t say presidents, I can’t say prime ministers, so I’m going to say Your Excellencies. (Laughter.) Let’s start with the issue that really must be preoccupying you from a national security point of view, which is the war in Ukraine. It doesn’t seem like much is changing on the battlefield. There are some indications that—recently that actually the Ukrainians have been doing well. On the other hand, the Russians have been able to destroy much of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. And they have these jet Shaheds that seem to be able to go faster and evade the Ukrainian efforts to intercept. How would you read the battlefront, to begin with?
STUBB: Well, I think there’s good news and bad news. The good news is that Ukraine is doing better politically, militarily, and financially than they have been doing at any time this year. I’d argue that they’ve been on top ever since December. On the battlefield, this means that the killing ratio is about one to five, one Ukrainian for five Russians. It means that since January Russia has advanced only 900 square kilometers, and Ukraine has taken back 800 square kilometers. It means that Ukraine is able to hit long-range targets, in terms of oil refineries and logistical centers. This is all good news. So it’s pretty much a stalemate.

The bad news, of course, is that winter is coming. And Ukraine right now desperately needs three things. One is air defense because, the ballistic missiles are coming through. Two is energy installments. And three is finances. So, you know, we’re working both to support Ukraine as best we can, together with Jonas and many others, and then on top of that we try to work with the peace negotiations as well.
ZAKARIA: Prime Minister, the big strategic reality that Ukraine faces economically has been the collapse of American support. American military assistance is essentially down to zero. The Europeans have stepped up extraordinarily, but now Ukraine says it has a $27 billion deficit. And it’s quite possible that this will get worse because, I was just in Ukraine, and the industrial economy has essentially shut down because of the—because of what President Stubb was saying. The energy infrastructure has been damaged badly enough that very few factories, big factories, are running. Do you think Europe will be able to do what it takes to support Ukraine?
STORE: Well, part of that finance is becoming more and more Northern European. I think that the Northern Europeans have stood, you know, the course until now. I think that the way Ukraine is resisting is telling us the following, how do wars end? They end when the warring parties see that, you know, the war is not going to deliver what they went into this, and the pain of the war is going to exceed what you can benefit from the war. I sense that we are getting closer to that point, in the sense that it’s a war that obviously should have not started. Every purpose that was defined when it started has not been achieved, basically. And now we’re five years into it soon, and it should stop.

So I think, yes, it will be critical during this winter. But I think, you know, the Ukrainians have shown us again and again their will to resist this. They are not going to lay down. The Donbas scenario, where President Putin, you know, he wants Donbas. There are 200,000 people living there. And Ukraine controls this area. And they will not give it up. They cannot give it up. It will be against their constitution. And no Ukrainian leader can give up a territory with people that they have died for. So that will not happen. So, you know, does that mean that we will approach a moment—and I think the president and I have, you know, been old colleagues in in foreign policy for almost twenty years now. We see that that moment must approach.
And that’s why I think the U.S., although, you know, I regret that there is not financial support. I think, you know, that’s a mistake. But they are critically important to get the diplomacy moving. So we need focus, and we will spend some time this week, I think, to make that voice heard. You know, to have an American role in that diplomacy to get it going. And then it will be our responsibility to see to it that Europe, which will have to live with the aftermath of this conflict. This is a conflict in our territory. Russia is our neighbor. That we can define a security structure for the future. But that moment has to come sooner than later, that there is a start of the end of this war.
ZAKARIA: President Stubb, you are sometimes called a Trump whisperer for the Europeans. You do have a good personal relationship with him. You talk to the negotiators often. Do you get the sense that there is any real movement on the negotiation side? Again, when I was in Kyiv the feeling was they were being—they were being given the same old offers, that there was no real progress.

STUBB: Well, I think, Jonas and I were there, I think, a week before you. And I think the mood then was rather positive. And we had spoken to the American negotiators a few times before they went in and right after they came out. And we spoke to president Zelensky, was it a week ago, a week and a half ago in in Oslo, and we’ll see him here this week. I think the fact that Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff went to Moscow, that John Ratcliffe went to Moscow, that was significant. And then that the two negotiators went to Kyiv got the ball rolling.
Now, my feeling is that out of those early negotiations there’s now sentiment that the Anchorage deal is out of the window, so three plus two doesn’t exist anymore.
ZAKARIA: Just explain what that is.
STUBB: And that means that the Russians wanted to take three of the oblasts and leave two to the Ukrainians. And this was their sort of assumption of the deal in Alaska. And this is out of the window. As is Ukrainian neutrality. And I think they are going to get back to so-called trilateral negotiations—Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S.—on a lower level, trying to get perhaps a partial deal, which would have to do something with the Black Sea, with grain corridors, and energy corridors. So my sense is that things are moving. Does this mean that we’re going to get peace immediately? No. But there has to come a point when, you know, the Russians realize that enough is enough and they will not have achieved their goals, which was to basically take over Ukraine, deny its independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity.

STORE: Now France is becoming very small in this context. (Laughter.) So cutting them down to size. So I use a map where I put, you know, this northern Arctic in the center. And this is what is happening, because with the melting ice, and with everything happening in terms of space development, the Arctic becomes geostrategically key. And again there, I think for us as small Arctic states, it is in our part of the Arctic that people live. The percent of Norwegian people live in the Arctic. So, you know, and on the Russian side. So maintaining, you know, order and stability there, there are a number of things we, as Arctic states, have to do to set the agenda.
Point one, there’s a legal order in the Arctic. The law of the sea applies. And the impression that this is a kind of _terra nullus_, where you can just come and grab land, that is not the case. So these principles have to be repeated. And there has to be, you know, we—NATO is, of course, covering all of NATO territory. Fifteen years ago Canada would not talk about the Arctic and NATO in the same context, because they wanted to keep their Arctic out of the security perspective. That has completely changed now. And with Prime Minister Carney, I was with him for the last day, and you were there a couple of weeks ago, we work strategically to integrate Arctic in the NATO defense posture.
So this is a work that I think is ongoing. And my kind of motivation is that we as, Arctic states, and I work very closely with Finland on this. We work together. We are bordering states. I said, we should always try to be one step ahead on ideas on how we do Arctic in a way which is, you know, taking care of our security. Because the rest of the world, not living in the Arctic, are more kind of searching. I heard President Trump said that, you know, he feared that Greenland was surrounded by Chinese and Russian ships. (Laughter.) This is not the case. (Laughter.) You know, Russia’s part is further in our corner, and China is growing interest in the Arctic, but they’re not there with ships twenty-four/seven. So let us be, you know, sober and focused on what the realities are. That’s the way we can maintain, you know, certain stability and low tension in the north.

ZAKARIA: President Stubb, you’re a scholar of international relations. One of the things people talk about a lot now is the breakdown of the post-1945 liberal order. And they say that, to a large extent, it is happening because of actions the United States is taking. The Trump administration is pulling out of various kinds of fora. In fact, they are now trying to, through various means, gut the International Criminal Court, even though they’re not part of it. They’ve withdrawn from a whole series of dozens and dozens of U.N. agencies. Is this an unraveling that can be reversed, should be reversed? How do you think of it? Or is this now the new normal?
STUBB: Well, I think actually the, quote/unquote, “unraveling” of the international order started earlier than Trump two. It started, in my mind, with Russia’s war of aggression in 2022, when a P5 member of the Security Council blatantly violates the U.N. Charter. And I think we should always look at the long game. We have a tendency, you know—
ZAKARIA: But, Mr. President, that’s happened before, the Korean War. The difference is that the United States then came to the rescue of that country, where now it seems like it’s abandoned it.
STUBB: It’s true. But what I mean when I say we need to look at the long game, we need to understand that this is a change in order, as we saw after World War One, World War Two, and the Cold War. I mean, you wrote, I think, a really good book, _The Post-American World_, already in the early 2000s, where you made an argument that we’re moving from multilateralism to multipolarity. And I agree with that thesis. And I still think that the choice stands. Now, is it a reality that the United States is not leaning into multilateral institutions anymore? Yes, it is a reality. In the WHO, with the ICC, with the climate accords, et cetera. et cetera. Now, how do we salvage the system is the key question.

And the answer that I’ve tried to push for is an understanding that the Global South or so-called middle powers will have a more important role and get agency in the institutions. That’s why, you know, in my U.N. speech, I will call for a new San Francisco moment, where the leaders of the United Nations, 193 of them, get together and figure out what the U.N. stands for, and what it should do. So I think there should be a rebalancing of power. Now, of course, that is only architectural tinkering. We also need the artisans to keep on working at this. And that’s why I think, you know, the next U.N. secretary-general will be very important in that she, or perhaps he, should become a big peace mediator. So, again, you know, I think it’ll take about five years for the system to settle. And, of course, the U.S. administration is accelerating that change, but it is not the only factor of that change.
ZAKARIA: Let me ask you a version of the same question, Prime Minister, because one of the things that has collapsed is the foreign aid regime that has, I would argue, helped many, many people in very desperate situations around the world. And now you have the reality of Sudan and South Sudan. You have, for example, an Ebola outbreak in Congo. And something like 5(00,000)-600,000 people are on the verge of starvation. And yet, aid budgets everywhere have been cut. The United States most dramatically shutting down USAID, but, as you know, many European countries have done the same. I ask because Norway is particularly generous and has continued to be generous.

STORE: Well, I think this is happening in a phase where also foreign aid is changing in nature, as it should. Because foreign aid, in terms of money, is very marginal in terms of supporting development in countries in development compared to direct investment, money coming back, and really supporting that. So, you know, if you want to help something—somebody out of poverty, would you give the money to the poorest people? No, not necessarily. You would give money so that economies can start to thrive. And I think one of the—I mean, having worked, myself, at the World Health Organization some twenty-five years ago, I was chief of staff under Dr. Brundtland when she was there as director-general. I saw that, you know, making strategic investments in health protect us, and it really makes the economy grow and thrive. And that’s where we should channel money.
So, in one way, I think it is right that foreign aid is being rethought and, you know, we do it in new ways. We are going through a major rethinking back home in Norway. We will maintain a high level, but we will do it differently, more strategically. So that, I think, is called for. Of course, the significant drop among main donors is negative, in the sense that you get less freeway to support those critical functions, like humanitarian aid, food aid, interventions in crisis. To me, just, you know, having observed it, the dismantlement of USAID is, to me, in our times the most striking self-hurting measure of your soft capital out there in the political world. Because I have seen in so many corners traveling around what that meant, and what extraordinary political investment it was in demonstrating that you can be—you can follow up in vulnerable places. Taking away the way that is. I think—but that—you know, that happens. And we have to move on.

And, you know, one of the reasons that we joined as the tenth country in the French initiative was basically to strengthen our deterrence and to create the strategic dilemma for some parts of the world. And we felt that if other Nordic countries are in this initiative—because Norway, Denmark, and Sweden had joined before us—we wanted to be a part of it. That is by no means a replacement of Article 5 and the U.S. nuclear umbrella. Quite the contrary. What we have committed to now is to begin a process with the French, because we understand that the French nuclear weapons are there to protect France, but we could give conventional backing in a crisis situation. So your assessment is correct. And, you know, had someone told me five years ago that we’d be NATO members and change our nuclear policy, I would have said I don’t think you know very much about international relations. (Laughter.)
ZAKARIA: Sir.
Q: Thank you very much for doing this. Elliot Waldman, editor-in-chief of _World Politics Review_.
There’s a strong case to be made that when it comes to NATO the currency of the realm is not warheads or drones or jets, but trust. And that that trust has been eroded in the Trump era. How do you think about the process of repair when it comes to that trust? How do you think about the process of rebuilding, perhaps post the Trump era? What will it take for the next American president to rebuild that trust? Or, on the other hand, has that ship sailed, and, you know, there’s a rupture now, and Europe has to think beyond its relationship with the U.S.?

STORE: Well, let me put it this way. I think, you know, the focus on statements by the American president grabbing the headlines and discussions, I can understand that. But let us look at some of the realities. The point that Europeans have to take greater charge of their own security is an old one. It’s not with Trump. I mean, go back many precedents. It’s always been on the agenda. Now it is happening. Now the Europeans are increasing their share to 3 ½, 5 percent. And they’re doing it according to updated regional plans. What does that mean? It means that we’re not going to reach 3.5, 3.5, 3.5, duplicating each other. We’re going to do it in an integrated way. The president mentioned number of fighter jets. If you put together Finland, Sweden, and Norway, you get to 250 of the most modern. And they are going to train and operate together to be not three separate forces, but when need comes it can integrate.
ZAKARIA: Now, can you get the French and the Germans to do the same thing? (Laughs.)
STORE: But here comes the point, Fareed. (Laughter.) And that is that what happens now in Europe, and this is for good reason, each region has to look after its own reality. And the Nordics—all Nordics in NATO, all Nordics in Norfolk, that’s a good thing, that command. Then you have what is called the Joint Expeditionary Force. It sounds very exciting, but it is basically Netherlands, U.K., Nordics, and Baltics coordinating their defense for issues which are a bit above what you can do on your own and a bit under the threshold of Article 5. We are integrating. And Canada is now wanting to join that cooperation, because this is the Northern European security posture.

The Polish prime minister and the German chancellor are both saying we have a Nordic perspective for our security, so they also should be included in that. So that is—you know, I think that is happening now. And we are—for Norway’s part, you know, we are buying our frigates from United Kingdom, which means that we will integrate our navies. We are buying our submarines from Germany. They are basically designed by Norwegians together with the Germans. And Canada will also buy those submarines. So we are integrating our navy. This is a new way of Europe taking responsibility. It doesn’t mean a new institution. The command structure is there in NATO. It is fully supported by SACEUR and by the American defense, you know, thinking. They have advanced thinking on this.
And then we have to respect—the Italian prime minister was in Oslo last week. And, you know, when she is coming to us to understand our reality, we also have to understand what it means to be around the Mediterranean. What is the threat posed from there? So I see that Europe is taking, you know, much further—much more advanced grip of its own security. In the EU, there is the program of supporting industry. Norway is also part of that, although we are not in the EU. But NATO is the command structure framework of how we work. And then, you know, as Alex is saying, you know, there is a re-posturing of American conventional troops. That’s been on the agenda for many, many years. And that has to happen in a way which is based on, you know, consultation. And that happens. So the change which we have been waiting for is happening now. And we don’t sit, you know, kind of silent, waiting for it to happen. We take active part.
ZAKARIA: OK, we have to wrap up but I want to just quickly ask each of you a question. There was a point at which you made a plea to President Trump to essentially tone down some of the belligerent rhetoric around Greenland, when he was moving in that direction. And he tweeted back saying, my dear Jonas, I would do this, but I have lost interest in peace ever since the Nobel Prize Committee refused to give me the Nobel Peace Prize. (Laughter.) You have publicly tried to explain this, but do you think that President Trump has been persuaded that you are not actually the person awarding the Nobel Peace Prize? (Laughter.)

STORE: Well, he can ask his colleague Xi Jinping coming to Washington next week, because China put Norway in the freezer because the Nobel Committee awarded the Peace Prize to a Chinese dissident. I think China knew that this is not a Norwegian government decision. This is a committee which is staunchly independent. They take that decision every year. In a few days, they will announce the prize for ’26. But China—
ZAKARIA: Can you give us some early indications? Is it Trump?
STORE: No, I get that news at the exact hour as the rest of the world. And I think, you know, President Trump’s advisers know. But, you know, that was at a quite critical moment, because this was something that Alex and I, again, did together.
STUBB: It was a joint text message, actually.
STORE: We were suggesting—it was a joint message that, ahead of Davos, we were kind of suggesting a trilateral talk between the three of us on the few issues—Ukraine and this issue—to see, you know, what we can achieve together. And then came this response. You know my response to that. You know, I reiterated that Norway is the place where Alfred Nobel said it should be the Norwegian Parliament that should appoint a committee that should award this prize. And that has happened since around 1900. It will continue. But that is what it means to be Norway. When there are reactions like that, either from China or from the American president, we will stand firm and say, this is how it is. This is the integrity of it. And, again, that’s how it is. (Laughter.)
ZAKARIA: Alex, I give you the last word on, do you think U.S.-European relations—there’s a possibility the midterm goes in a direction that President Trump will not like. In any case, presidents in their last two years often focus on foreign policy because that’s an area outside of congressional control. What do you expect President Trump to focus on in the next two years in foreign policy?

degrade these features, which are central to what makes our society  
worth defending in the first place.
Democracy is a fundamental component of creating a just society  
providing a mechanism for the governed to select their leaders and  
participate in decision-making. A just society is better and more stable  
than an unjust one (although the transition to democracy can be  
destabilizing). The rule of law and civil liberty promote and protect  
equality and liberty and create the political climate of trust necessary  
for the connections of modern life to thrive. Education and adequate  
economic well-being are crucial for the human spirit to flourish. Lack  
of access to education and social exclusion or degradation undermine  
cohesion. Pluralism is particularly important, but not well understood.  
Pluralism defends a diversity of cultural and religious expressions  
within a framework of tolerance guided by certain rules. Pluralism  
requires that all accept certain principles, including respect for  
others. Unlike multiculturalism, which tends to confine people in sep-  
arate cultural traditions, the concept of pluralism better allows each  
person to fulfill complex multiple identities while maintaining overall  
cohesion.
The elements of physical protection include infrastructure, public  
health, natural disaster relief, environmental quality and anti-terror-  
ism measures aimed at thwarting attacks within the U.S. In my socie-  
tal security model, fighting terrorism is portrayed as a crosscutting  
policy, not a fundamental sphere of security. Fighting terrorism is an  
important policy action, but it should not be the defining framework  
for our strategic outlook.
We can draw on several theoretical traditions to understand how to  
arrange priorities within the concept of societal security. Our efforts
texts.96:
## [PDF page 67]
32  Transforming Homeland Security
to enhance human safety can benefit from a rich theoretical tradition  
that endeavors to highlight the role of the individual person in inter-  
national affairs. In this section I will draw from four traditions: com-  
mon security, human needs, human security and Nordic notions of  
societal security. The first three emerge from policy debates within  
the economic development community. From their efforts to define  
the good society and hence the ultimate goal of development, devel-  
opment experts honed useful concepts about ways to enhance human  
well-being that can help us understand which themes are most  
important when developing our notion of human safety within socie-  
tal security.
In the latter portion of the Cold War, there were significant efforts  
to recover notions of human value amid the overwhelming concern  
with state security and the threat of nuclear war between the super-  
powers. In their reports North-South: A Program for Survival  (1980)  
and  Common Crisis: North-South Cooperation for World Recovery  (1983),  
the Independent Commission on International Development Issues  
led by former German chancellor Willy Brandt sought to connect  
development issues and strategic world order concerns. The Brandt  
Commission discussed the interplay between social issues that directly  
affect people such as hunger, poverty, and human rights with interna-  
tional economic and security affairs. The related notion of common  
security derives from a celebrated international report of the same  
name issued by the Independent Commission on Disarmament and  
Security Issues in 1982. This commission led by Swedish Prime  
Minister Olaf Palme stressed that both East and West had a common  
interest in safety and that security had to be achieved together.9  Taken  
together these well-publicized reports by political leaders raised the  
idea that security needed to include the well-being of people.
The notion that national policies needed to connect to people’ s  
well-being was advanced further by the concept of “basic needs.”

## [PDF page 68]
From Territorial Security to Societal Security  33
Again, ferment within the development community produced an idea  
that economic development needed to be geared towards the funda-  
mental elements that sustained human life, not just towards large  
infrastructure projects. Thus, reducing poverty and hunger or increas-  
ing literacy were just (or even more) valid measures than the number  
of highways or bridges built. If economic development can be linked  
to human well-being, then the notion that security can be connected  
to human safety is not a big step.
The third framework discussed here, human security, endeavors to  
make a direct connection between personal safety and national secu-  
rity. Concepts of human security can help us prioritize what features  
must be maintained for human well-being. Human security endeavors  
to use the person rather the state as the unit to be safeguarded, but it  
also acknowledges that people need social constructs for well-being  
(provision of food, maintenance of health, etc.).
There have been several efforts to define human security. Indeed,  
the idea suffers from significant theoretical imprecision.10  However,  
within the more coherent expressions of the idea certain core notions  
can be discerned. The concept of human security appears in a 1994  
report by the United Nations Development Program (UNDP).  
Scholars such as Gary King and Christopher Murray tried to analyze  
the idea more deeply. Meanwhile, the Canadian and other govern-  
ments tried to translate the theory into policy. There was even a  
report on human security by a distinguished international panel  
headed by the former UN High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako  
Ogata and Nobel laureate Amartya Sen.11  Each analysis has a some-  
what different definition. Table 1 lists definitions of human security  
according to the UNDP, King and Murray, and my definition.
10  Roland Paris, “Human Security: Paradigm Shift or Hot Air,” International Security  26 (Fall  
2001): p. 99.

Highlights of the interview were broadcast on CNN’s _Fareed Zakaria GPS_ on Sunday, September 27 at 10:00 a.m. (EDT), with a planned replay at 1:00 p.m. (EDT).
ZAKARIA: All right. I’d like to welcome all of you. We have, of course, very distinguished guests with us today—the Prime Minister of Norway, the president of Finland.
This is called the Russell Leffingwell Lecture. And we do want to thank the Leffingwell family for their generosity in endowing this lecture, especially Tom and Ted Leffingwell Pulling. Appreciate it greatly. Russell Leffingwell was a charter member of the CFR who also served as its president from 1944 to ’46, and its chairman from ’46 to ’53.
You know the usual rules for the Council apply. We will begin with a conversation, and then about halfway through I’ll open it up to questions.
Welcome—I can’t say presidents, I can’t say prime ministers, so I’m going to say Your Excellencies. (Laughter.) Let’s start with the issue that really must be preoccupying you from a national security point of view, which is the war in Ukraine. It doesn’t seem like much is changing on the battlefield. There are some indications that—recently that actually the Ukrainians have been doing well. On the other hand, the Russians have been able to destroy much of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. And they have these jet Shaheds that seem to be able to go faster and evade the Ukrainian efforts to intercept. How would you read the battlefront, to begin with?
STUBB: Well, I think there’s good news and bad news. The good news is that Ukraine is doing better politically, militarily, and financially than they have been doing at any time this year. I’d argue that they’ve been on top ever since December. On the battlefield, this means that the killing ratio is about one to five, one Ukrainian for five Russians. It means that since January Russia has advanced only 900 square kilometers, and Ukraine has taken back 800 square kilometers. It means that Ukraine is able to hit long-range targets, in terms of oil refineries and logistical centers. This is all good news. So it’s pretty much a stalemate.
texts.1:
The bad news, of course, is that winter is coming. And Ukraine right now desperately needs three things. One is air defense because, the ballistic missiles are coming through. Two is energy installments. And three is finances. So, you know, we’re working both to support Ukraine as best we can, together with Jonas and many others, and then on top of that we try to work with the peace negotiations as well.
ZAKARIA: Prime Minister, the big strategic reality that Ukraine faces economically has been the collapse of American support. American military assistance is essentially down to zero. The Europeans have stepped up extraordinarily, but now Ukraine says it has a $27 billion deficit. And it’s quite possible that this will get worse because, I was just in Ukraine, and the industrial economy has essentially shut down because of the—because of what President Stubb was saying. The energy infrastructure has been damaged badly enough that very few factories, big factories, are running. Do you think Europe will be able to do what it takes to support Ukraine?
STORE: Well, part of that finance is becoming more and more Northern European. I think that the Northern Europeans have stood, you know, the course until now. I think that the way Ukraine is resisting is telling us the following, how do wars end? They end when the warring parties see that, you know, the war is not going to deliver what they went into this, and the pain of the war is going to exceed what you can benefit from the war. I sense that we are getting closer to that point, in the sense that it’s a war that obviously should have not started. Every purpose that was defined when it started has not been achieved, basically. And now we’re five years into it soon, and it should stop.
texts.2:
So I think, yes, it will be critical during this winter. But I think, you know, the Ukrainians have shown us again and again their will to resist this. They are not going to lay down. The Donbas scenario, where President Putin, you know, he wants Donbas. There are 200,000 people living there. And Ukraine controls this area. And they will not give it up. They cannot give it up. It will be against their constitution. And no Ukrainian leader can give up a territory with people that they have died for. So that will not happen. So, you know, does that mean that we will approach a moment—and I think the president and I have, you know, been old colleagues in in foreign policy for almost twenty years now. We see that that moment must approach.
And that’s why I think the U.S., although, you know, I regret that there is not financial support. I think, you know, that’s a mistake. But they are critically important to get the diplomacy moving. So we need focus, and we will spend some time this week, I think, to make that voice heard. You know, to have an American role in that diplomacy to get it going. And then it will be our responsibility to see to it that Europe, which will have to live with the aftermath of this conflict. This is a conflict in our territory. Russia is our neighbor. That we can define a security structure for the future. But that moment has to come sooner than later, that there is a start of the end of this war.
ZAKARIA: President Stubb, you are sometimes called a Trump whisperer for the Europeans. You do have a good personal relationship with him. You talk to the negotiators often. Do you get the sense that there is any real movement on the negotiation side? Again, when I was in Kyiv the feeling was they were being—they were being given the same old offers, that there was no real progress.
texts.3:
STUBB: Well, I think, Jonas and I were there, I think, a week before you. And I think the mood then was rather positive. And we had spoken to the American negotiators a few times before they went in and right after they came out. And we spoke to president Zelensky, was it a week ago, a week and a half ago in in Oslo, and we’ll see him here this week. I think the fact that Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff went to Moscow, that John Ratcliffe went to Moscow, that was significant. And then that the two negotiators went to Kyiv got the ball rolling.
Now, my feeling is that out of those early negotiations there’s now sentiment that the Anchorage deal is out of the window, so three plus two doesn’t exist anymore.
ZAKARIA: Just explain what that is.
STUBB: And that means that the Russians wanted to take three of the oblasts and leave two to the Ukrainians. And this was their sort of assumption of the deal in Alaska. And this is out of the window. As is Ukrainian neutrality. And I think they are going to get back to so-called trilateral negotiations—Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S.—on a lower level, trying to get perhaps a partial deal, which would have to do something with the Black Sea, with grain corridors, and energy corridors. So my sense is that things are moving. Does this mean that we’re going to get peace immediately? No. But there has to come a point when, you know, the Russians realize that enough is enough and they will not have achieved their goals, which was to basically take over Ukraine, deny its independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity.
texts.9:
STORE: Now France is becoming very small in this context. (Laughter.) So cutting them down to size. So I use a map where I put, you know, this northern Arctic in the center. And this is what is happening, because with the melting ice, and with everything happening in terms of space development, the Arctic becomes geostrategically key. And again there, I think for us as small Arctic states, it is in our part of the Arctic that people live. The percent of Norwegian people live in the Arctic. So, you know, and on the Russian side. So maintaining, you know, order and stability there, there are a number of things we, as Arctic states, have to do to set the agenda.
Point one, there’s a legal order in the Arctic. The law of the sea applies. And the impression that this is a kind of _terra nullus_, where you can just come and grab land, that is not the case. So these principles have to be repeated. And there has to be, you know, we—NATO is, of course, covering all of NATO territory. Fifteen years ago Canada would not talk about the Arctic and NATO in the same context, because they wanted to keep their Arctic out of the security perspective. That has completely changed now. And with Prime Minister Carney, I was with him for the last day, and you were there a couple of weeks ago, we work strategically to integrate Arctic in the NATO defense posture.
So this is a work that I think is ongoing. And my kind of motivation is that we as, Arctic states, and I work very closely with Finland on this. We work together. We are bordering states. I said, we should always try to be one step ahead on ideas on how we do Arctic in a way which is, you know, taking care of our security. Because the rest of the world, not living in the Arctic, are more kind of searching. I heard President Trump said that, you know, he feared that Greenland was surrounded by Chinese and Russian ships. (Laughter.) This is not the case. (Laughter.) You know, Russia’s part is further in our corner, and China is growing interest in the Arctic, but they’re not there with ships twenty-four/seven. So let us be, you know, sober and focused on what the realities are. That’s the way we can maintain, you know, certain stability and low tension in the north.
texts.10:
ZAKARIA: President Stubb, you’re a scholar of international relations. One of the things people talk about a lot now is the breakdown of the post-1945 liberal order. And they say that, to a large extent, it is happening because of actions the United States is taking. The Trump administration is pulling out of various kinds of fora. In fact, they are now trying to, through various means, gut the International Criminal Court, even though they’re not part of it. They’ve withdrawn from a whole series of dozens and dozens of U.N. agencies. Is this an unraveling that can be reversed, should be reversed? How do you think of it? Or is this now the new normal?
STUBB: Well, I think actually the, quote/unquote, “unraveling” of the international order started earlier than Trump two. It started, in my mind, with Russia’s war of aggression in 2022, when a P5 member of the Security Council blatantly violates the U.N. Charter. And I think we should always look at the long game. We have a tendency, you know—
ZAKARIA: But, Mr. President, that’s happened before, the Korean War. The difference is that the United States then came to the rescue of that country, where now it seems like it’s abandoned it.
STUBB: It’s true. But what I mean when I say we need to look at the long game, we need to understand that this is a change in order, as we saw after World War One, World War Two, and the Cold War. I mean, you wrote, I think, a really good book, _The Post-American World_, already in the early 2000s, where you made an argument that we’re moving from multilateralism to multipolarity. And I agree with that thesis. And I still think that the choice stands. Now, is it a reality that the United States is not leaning into multilateral institutions anymore? Yes, it is a reality. In the WHO, with the ICC, with the climate accords, et cetera. et cetera. Now, how do we salvage the system is the key question.
texts.11:
And the answer that I’ve tried to push for is an understanding that the Global South or so-called middle powers will have a more important role and get agency in the institutions. That’s why, you know, in my U.N. speech, I will call for a new San Francisco moment, where the leaders of the United Nations, 193 of them, get together and figure out what the U.N. stands for, and what it should do. So I think there should be a rebalancing of power. Now, of course, that is only architectural tinkering. We also need the artisans to keep on working at this. And that’s why I think, you know, the next U.N. secretary-general will be very important in that she, or perhaps he, should become a big peace mediator. So, again, you know, I think it’ll take about five years for the system to settle. And, of course, the U.S. administration is accelerating that change, but it is not the only factor of that change.
ZAKARIA: Let me ask you a version of the same question, Prime Minister, because one of the things that has collapsed is the foreign aid regime that has, I would argue, helped many, many people in very desperate situations around the world. And now you have the reality of Sudan and South Sudan. You have, for example, an Ebola outbreak in Congo. And something like 5(00,000)-600,000 people are on the verge of starvation. And yet, aid budgets everywhere have been cut. The United States most dramatically shutting down USAID, but, as you know, many European countries have done the same. I ask because Norway is particularly generous and has continued to be generous.
texts.12:
STORE: Well, I think this is happening in a phase where also foreign aid is changing in nature, as it should. Because foreign aid, in terms of money, is very marginal in terms of supporting development in countries in development compared to direct investment, money coming back, and really supporting that. So, you know, if you want to help something—somebody out of poverty, would you give the money to the poorest people? No, not necessarily. You would give money so that economies can start to thrive. And I think one of the—I mean, having worked, myself, at the World Health Organization some twenty-five years ago, I was chief of staff under Dr. Brundtland when she was there as director-general. I saw that, you know, making strategic investments in health protect us, and it really makes the economy grow and thrive. And that’s where we should channel money.
So, in one way, I think it is right that foreign aid is being rethought and, you know, we do it in new ways. We are going through a major rethinking back home in Norway. We will maintain a high level, but we will do it differently, more strategically. So that, I think, is called for. Of course, the significant drop among main donors is negative, in the sense that you get less freeway to support those critical functions, like humanitarian aid, food aid, interventions in crisis. To me, just, you know, having observed it, the dismantlement of USAID is, to me, in our times the most striking self-hurting measure of your soft capital out there in the political world. Because I have seen in so many corners traveling around what that meant, and what extraordinary political investment it was in demonstrating that you can be—you can follow up in vulnerable places. Taking away the way that is. I think—but that—you know, that happens. And we have to move on.
texts.25:
And, you know, one of the reasons that we joined as the tenth country in the French initiative was basically to strengthen our deterrence and to create the strategic dilemma for some parts of the world. And we felt that if other Nordic countries are in this initiative—because Norway, Denmark, and Sweden had joined before us—we wanted to be a part of it. That is by no means a replacement of Article 5 and the U.S. nuclear umbrella. Quite the contrary. What we have committed to now is to begin a process with the French, because we understand that the French nuclear weapons are there to protect France, but we could give conventional backing in a crisis situation. So your assessment is correct. And, you know, had someone told me five years ago that we’d be NATO members and change our nuclear policy, I would have said I don’t think you know very much about international relations. (Laughter.)
ZAKARIA: Sir.
Q: Thank you very much for doing this. Elliot Waldman, editor-in-chief of _World Politics Review_.
There’s a strong case to be made that when it comes to NATO the currency of the realm is not warheads or drones or jets, but trust. And that that trust has been eroded in the Trump era. How do you think about the process of repair when it comes to that trust? How do you think about the process of rebuilding, perhaps post the Trump era? What will it take for the next American president to rebuild that trust? Or, on the other hand, has that ship sailed, and, you know, there’s a rupture now, and Europe has to think beyond its relationship with the U.S.?
texts.26:
STORE: Well, let me put it this way. I think, you know, the focus on statements by the American president grabbing the headlines and discussions, I can understand that. But let us look at some of the realities. The point that Europeans have to take greater charge of their own security is an old one. It’s not with Trump. I mean, go back many precedents. It’s always been on the agenda. Now it is happening. Now the Europeans are increasing their share to 3 ½, 5 percent. And they’re doing it according to updated regional plans. What does that mean? It means that we’re not going to reach 3.5, 3.5, 3.5, duplicating each other. We’re going to do it in an integrated way. The president mentioned number of fighter jets. If you put together Finland, Sweden, and Norway, you get to 250 of the most modern. And they are going to train and operate together to be not three separate forces, but when need comes it can integrate.
ZAKARIA: Now, can you get the French and the Germans to do the same thing? (Laughs.)
STORE: But here comes the point, Fareed. (Laughter.) And that is that what happens now in Europe, and this is for good reason, each region has to look after its own reality. And the Nordics—all Nordics in NATO, all Nordics in Norfolk, that’s a good thing, that command. Then you have what is called the Joint Expeditionary Force. It sounds very exciting, but it is basically Netherlands, U.K., Nordics, and Baltics coordinating their defense for issues which are a bit above what you can do on your own and a bit under the threshold of Article 5. We are integrating. And Canada is now wanting to join that cooperation, because this is the Northern European security posture.
texts.27:
The Polish prime minister and the German chancellor are both saying we have a Nordic perspective for our security, so they also should be included in that. So that is—you know, I think that is happening now. And we are—for Norway’s part, you know, we are buying our frigates from United Kingdom, which means that we will integrate our navies. We are buying our submarines from Germany. They are basically designed by Norwegians together with the Germans. And Canada will also buy those submarines. So we are integrating our navy. This is a new way of Europe taking responsibility. It doesn’t mean a new institution. The command structure is there in NATO. It is fully supported by SACEUR and by the American defense, you know, thinking. They have advanced thinking on this.
And then we have to respect—the Italian prime minister was in Oslo last week. And, you know, when she is coming to us to understand our reality, we also have to understand what it means to be around the Mediterranean. What is the threat posed from there? So I see that Europe is taking, you know, much further—much more advanced grip of its own security. In the EU, there is the program of supporting industry. Norway is also part of that, although we are not in the EU. But NATO is the command structure framework of how we work. And then, you know, as Alex is saying, you know, there is a re-posturing of American conventional troops. That’s been on the agenda for many, many years. And that has to happen in a way which is based on, you know, consultation. And that happens. So the change which we have been waiting for is happening now. And we don’t sit, you know, kind of silent, waiting for it to happen. We take active part.
ZAKARIA: OK, we have to wrap up but I want to just quickly ask each of you a question. There was a point at which you made a plea to President Trump to essentially tone down some of the belligerent rhetoric around Greenland, when he was moving in that direction. And he tweeted back saying, my dear Jonas, I would do this, but I have lost interest in peace ever since the Nobel Prize Committee refused to give me the Nobel Peace Prize. (Laughter.) You have publicly tried to explain this, but do you think that President Trump has been persuaded that you are not actually the person awarding the Nobel Peace Prize? (Laughter.)
texts.28:
STORE: Well, he can ask his colleague Xi Jinping coming to Washington next week, because China put Norway in the freezer because the Nobel Committee awarded the Peace Prize to a Chinese dissident. I think China knew that this is not a Norwegian government decision. This is a committee which is staunchly independent. They take that decision every year. In a few days, they will announce the prize for ’26. But China—
ZAKARIA: Can you give us some early indications? Is it Trump?
STORE: No, I get that news at the exact hour as the rest of the world. And I think, you know, President Trump’s advisers know. But, you know, that was at a quite critical moment, because this was something that Alex and I, again, did together.
STUBB: It was a joint text message, actually.
STORE: We were suggesting—it was a joint message that, ahead of Davos, we were kind of suggesting a trilateral talk between the three of us on the few issues—Ukraine and this issue—to see, you know, what we can achieve together. And then came this response. You know my response to that. You know, I reiterated that Norway is the place where Alfred Nobel said it should be the Norwegian Parliament that should appoint a committee that should award this prize. And that has happened since around 1900. It will continue. But that is what it means to be Norway. When there are reactions like that, either from China or from the American president, we will stand firm and say, this is how it is. This is the integrity of it. And, again, that’s how it is. (Laughter.)
ZAKARIA: Alex, I give you the last word on, do you think U.S.-European relations—there’s a possibility the midterm goes in a direction that President Trump will not like. In any case, presidents in their last two years often focus on foreign policy because that’s an area outside of congressional control. What do you expect President Trump to focus on in the next two years in foreign policy?

**Hero of Belarus** (Belarusian: Герой Беларусі, Łacinka_Hieroj Biełarusi_; Russian: Герой Беларуси, romanized:_Geroj Belarusi_) is the highest title that can be bestowed on a citizen of Belarus. The title is awarded to those "who perform great deeds in the name of freedom, independence and prosperity of the Republic of Belarus".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-N3599-2) The deed can be for military performance, economic performance or great service to the State and society. The design of the medal is similar to that of its predecessor, Hero of the Soviet Union. Similar titles to the Hero of Belarus include the Hero of the Russian Federation, Hero of Ukraine, and Hero of Uzbekistan. Since its creation, the title has been awarded to eleven people.

The title and other Belarusian state awards, their creation, nomination and awarding, are regulated by a set of legal documents: Belarusian Constitution, Law N 288-З "About state awards of the Republic of Belarus" and presidential decrees.
The title was created by the Belarus Supreme Soviet on April 13, 1995, with the passage of Resolution N 3726-XII, titled "System of State Awards for the Republic of Belarus". Alongside the Hero of Belarus title, the resolution authorized the creation of medals, orders, and titles that can be presented by the Belarusian government. The creation of the awards was a way to honor those who have made valuable contributions to Belarus, irrespective of whether they were performed by a citizen or a foreigner.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-N3726-3)
This resolution was outlawed and replaced by Law N 288-З on May 18, 2004.

## Recommendation process and awarding
[edit]
To be considered for title, a person must perform a deed that greatly benefits the state and Belarusian society at large. The title can be awarded to those serving in the military, public service or private enterprise. It can only be awarded once to an individual, and can be awarded posthumously. The official criteria are stated in Chapter 2, Article 5 of Law N 288-З. Chapter 3, Article 60 of Law N 288-З allows any group (association) of workers to submit a recommendation (petition) for an individual to be awarded the title. Governmental bodies, the National Assembly, the Council of Ministers, cabinet officials and public unions, among others, are also eligible to submit nominations for the title. The candidate is evaluated, and if deemed worthy, the nomination is forwarded to the Council of Ministers and then, after having been allowed by the Governmental Secretariat of the Belarusian Security Council, to the President of the Republic.
Under the Belarus Constitution (Part 4, Chapter 3, Article 84), the President of the Republic has the power to bestow state awards. To announce an award, the President issues a decree conferring the title to a person.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-const-4) Within two months, the title will be presented by the President in a formal setting, usually at the Independence Palace in the capital city of Minsk. A certificate (_gramota_) will also be presented to the recipient, signed by the President of the Republic.
Initially, social privileges for those, who achieved Hero of Belarus, according to the Resolution of the Supreme Council of the Republic of Belarus under April 13, 1995 N 3727-XII,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-5) were equal to the privileges for people, whom Hero of Soviet Union, Hero of Socialist Labour, Order of Glory or Order of Labor Glory was given. These privileges are regulated by Resolution of the Supreme Council of the Republic of Belarus under February 21, 1995 N 3599-XII.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-N3599-2)

## Recommendation process and awarding
Now this question is regulated by Law of the Republic of Belarus under June 14, 2007 N 239-З "About social privileges, rights and guarantees to a definite category of citizens".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-6)
According to it, Heroes of Belarus have rights:
*   of free supplying with medicines in the list of main medicines, which are given under recipes in hospitals;  
*   of free production and repairing of dentures in governmental organizations domiciliary and of free supplying with other technical means of rehabilitation in accordance with the Governmental register of technical means of social rehabilitation;  
*   of pecuniary aid for recovery or, instead of pecuniary aid, of free out-of-turn sanitary-resort recovery;  
*   of free trip on all kinds of urban transport (except taxi) irrespective of domicile;  
*   of free trip on the transport (railway, water, auto, but not taxi) of suburban traffic;  
*   of one free roundtrip by rail, airplane, or truck per year of interurban traffic;  
*   rent-free housing, utilities, and services within 20 square meters of living space;  
*   of free home phone installation if the extension of the subscriber line is less than 500 meters;  
*   of free usage of the home phone (except interurban and international talks).
The consumptions, connected with these privileges, are financed from means of republican and local budgets and of governmental social insurance.

## Construction and display
[edit]
1996–1999 medal
The recipient of the title is given a medal called the Medal of the Hero of Belarus (Belarusian: медаль Героя Беларусі, Russian: медаль Героя Беларуси). The star and suspension are made of gold, and thus it is nicknamed "Gold Star", as was its predecessor, the Hero of the Soviet Union. The star has a total diameter of 33 millimeters, and is attached to a rectangular suspension device (boot tree). In the center of the rectangle is a ribbon of two sections of red and one section of green. The red and green bars on the ribbon evoke the design and colors of the national flag. The amount of gold is set at 585–1 Test, with the total weight of the medal being 19grams.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-medal-7) The present design was enacted into law by Presidential Decree Number 516 on September 6, 1999.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-8)
The design of the medal is modeled after one used for the Hero of the Soviet Union. Unlike the Hero of the Soviet Union, Hero of Socialist Labor and the Hero of the Russian Federation titles, there is no engraving on the reverse of the star. The ribbon also copies the Soviet Hero medal's ribbon, since a flag design was also used to make the ribbon of that medal. The medal is always worn in full on the left side of the breast above all other medals and orders. Chapter 4, Article 69 of Law N 288-З states that any awards and titles presented by the Soviet Union and the Byelorussian SSR must be placed after awards from the Republic of Belarus.

## Construction and display
When the title was created, a suggested medal was drafted and designed by the government. The major difference between this medal and the current medal is the design of the suspension and the star medallion at the bottom: the top suspension is longer than the bottom, and the bottom star is outlined differently and is adorned with rubies. The suspension was made from gold-plated silver, while the suspension of the current medal is made from gold, as the medal. The design of the star evokes the [Marshal's Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshal's_Star "Marshal's Star"), which Soviet Marshals wore around their necks. This medal was adopted by Presidential Decree Number 26 on May 15, 1996.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-belawards-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-10)

The first "group awarding" took place on June 30, 2001 to Pavel Mariev, Mikhail Karchmit, Vital Kramko and Alaksandar Dubko (posthumous),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-sb-11) while Kirill Vakhromeev, Mikhail Savitsky, Mikhail Vysotsky, Pyotr Prakapovich and Vasil Ravyaka were presented their titles on March 1, 2006.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-%D0%93%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B8_%D0%91%D0%B5%D0%BB%D0%B0%D1%80%D1%83%D1%81%D0%B8-1)

## Construction and display
Uladzimir Karvat, a military pilot, was flying his training aircraft Sukhoi Su-27 on May 23, 1996. The plane caught fire and Karvat was ordered to eject to safety. Unknown to the ground crew, the plane would have crashed in an area full of civilians. Seeing the civilians on the ground, Karvat steered the plane away until it crashed one kilometer from the Brest Region settlements of Arabawshchyna and Vyalikaye Hatsishcha, killing him instantly. President Alexander Lukashenko issued Decree Number 484 on November 21, 1996, which posthumously awarded Karvat the title Hero of Belarus.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-karvat-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-13) The crash site has been converted to a memorial for Karvat, where a copy of Lukashenko's decree is on the tail fin of the Sukhoi Su-27p.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-memorial-14)
Pavel Mariev was awarded the title for his work in the automobile industry as manager of Belarusian Auto Works, a leading producer of Belarusian automobiles.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-15)
Vital Kramko and Mikhail Karchmit were awarded for their work in the agriculture industry. Kramko is the chairman of the Grodno Region agricultural collective "October", while Karchmit was the director of the Minsk Region cooperative "Snov" until his death in 2004.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-karcmit-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-17)

**Hero of Belarus** (Belarusian: Герой Беларусі, Łacinka_Hieroj Biełarusi_; Russian: Герой Беларуси, romanized:_Geroj Belarusi_) is the highest title that can be bestowed on a citizen of Belarus. The title is awarded to those "who perform great deeds in the name of freedom, independence and prosperity of the Republic of Belarus".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-N3599-2) The deed can be for military performance, economic performance or great service to the State and society. The design of the medal is similar to that of its predecessor, Hero of the Soviet Union. Similar titles to the Hero of Belarus include the Hero of the Russian Federation, Hero of Ukraine, and Hero of Uzbekistan. Since its creation, the title has been awarded to eleven people.
texts.1:
The title and other Belarusian state awards, their creation, nomination and awarding, are regulated by a set of legal documents: Belarusian Constitution, Law N 288-З "About state awards of the Republic of Belarus" and presidential decrees.
The title was created by the Belarus Supreme Soviet on April 13, 1995, with the passage of Resolution N 3726-XII, titled "System of State Awards for the Republic of Belarus". Alongside the Hero of Belarus title, the resolution authorized the creation of medals, orders, and titles that can be presented by the Belarusian government. The creation of the awards was a way to honor those who have made valuable contributions to Belarus, irrespective of whether they were performed by a citizen or a foreigner.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-N3726-3)
This resolution was outlawed and replaced by Law N 288-З on May 18, 2004.

## Recommendation process and awarding
[edit]
To be considered for title, a person must perform a deed that greatly benefits the state and Belarusian society at large. The title can be awarded to those serving in the military, public service or private enterprise. It can only be awarded once to an individual, and can be awarded posthumously. The official criteria are stated in Chapter 2, Article 5 of Law N 288-З. Chapter 3, Article 60 of Law N 288-З allows any group (association) of workers to submit a recommendation (petition) for an individual to be awarded the title. Governmental bodies, the National Assembly, the Council of Ministers, cabinet officials and public unions, among others, are also eligible to submit nominations for the title. The candidate is evaluated, and if deemed worthy, the nomination is forwarded to the Council of Ministers and then, after having been allowed by the Governmental Secretariat of the Belarusian Security Council, to the President of the Republic.
Under the Belarus Constitution (Part 4, Chapter 3, Article 84), the President of the Republic has the power to bestow state awards. To announce an award, the President issues a decree conferring the title to a person.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-const-4) Within two months, the title will be presented by the President in a formal setting, usually at the Independence Palace in the capital city of Minsk. A certificate (_gramota_) will also be presented to the recipient, signed by the President of the Republic.
Initially, social privileges for those, who achieved Hero of Belarus, according to the Resolution of the Supreme Council of the Republic of Belarus under April 13, 1995 N 3727-XII,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-5) were equal to the privileges for people, whom Hero of Soviet Union, Hero of Socialist Labour, Order of Glory or Order of Labor Glory was given. These privileges are regulated by Resolution of the Supreme Council of the Republic of Belarus under February 21, 1995 N 3599-XII.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-N3599-2)

## Construction and display
Uladzimir Karvat, a military pilot, was flying his training aircraft Sukhoi Su-27 on May 23, 1996. The plane caught fire and Karvat was ordered to eject to safety. Unknown to the ground crew, the plane would have crashed in an area full of civilians. Seeing the civilians on the ground, Karvat steered the plane away until it crashed one kilometer from the Brest Region settlements of Arabawshchyna and Vyalikaye Hatsishcha, killing him instantly. President Alexander Lukashenko issued Decree Number 484 on November 21, 1996, which posthumously awarded Karvat the title Hero of Belarus.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-karvat-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-13) The crash site has been converted to a memorial for Karvat, where a copy of Lukashenko's decree is on the tail fin of the Sukhoi Su-27p.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-memorial-14)
Pavel Mariev was awarded the title for his work in the automobile industry as manager of Belarusian Auto Works, a leading producer of Belarusian automobiles.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-15)
Vital Kramko and Mikhail Karchmit were awarded for their work in the agriculture industry. Kramko is the chairman of the Grodno Region agricultural collective "October", while Karchmit was the director of the Minsk Region cooperative "Snov" until his death in 2004.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-karcmit-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-17)

The star and suspension are made of gold, and thus it is nicknamed "Gold Star", as was its predecessor, the Hero of the Soviet Union. The star has a total diameter of 33 millimeters, and is attached to a rectangular suspension device (boot tree). The design of the medal is modeled after one used for the Hero of the Soviet Union. Unlike the Hero of the Soviet Union, Hero of Socialist Labor and the Hero of the Russian Federation titles, there is no engraving on the reverse of the star. The ribbon also copies the Soviet Hero medal's ribbon, since a flag design was also used to make the ribbon of that medal. The medal is always worn in full on the left side of the breast above all other medals and orders. Chapter 4, Article 69 of Law N 288-З states that any awards and titles presented by the Soviet Union and the Byelorussian SSR must be placed after awards from the Republic of Belarus.[[2]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-Law288-2) The same one can reed in the Presidential decree N 168 on April 8, 2005.[[10]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Hero_of_Belarus#cite_note-10)

"We are all in it together. This is a war. We take a few shots and it will be over. We will give them a few shots and it will be over. Don't worry. I wouldn't want to be on the other side right now....I want the most comprehensive notes on all those who tried to do us in. They didn't have to do it. If we had had a very close election and they were playing the other side I would understand this. No—they were doing this quite deliberately and they are asking for it and they are going to get it....We have not used the Bureau, and we have not used the Justice Department, but things are going to change now....And who the hell are they after? Transcript of President Nixon speaking to John Dean in the Oval Office, September 5,1972
U.S. Congress, House. National Archives.

a. Growing public opposition to and protests against the Vietnam War

Political scandals and clashes over the power of the presidency

the power of the presidency and the federal government.

"The Declaration of Independence, signed in 1776, stated that 'all Men are created equal' and that governments derive their powers 'from the Consent of the Governed.' Women were not included in either concept. The original American Constitution of 1787 was founded on English common law, which did not recognize women as citizens or as individuals with legal rights....It has been argued that the ERA is not necessary because the Fourteenth Amendment...guarantees that no state shall deny to 'any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws.'...Aside from the fact that women have been subjected to varying, inconsistent, and often unfavorable decisions under the Fourteenth Amendment, the Equal Rights Amendment is a more immediate and effective remedy to sex discrimination in Federal and State laws than case-by-case interpretation under the Fourteenth Amendment could ever be."

a. groups on the left assailing the status quo in American society.

d. Supreme Court decisions expanding individual freedoms.
conservatives and liberals clashing over the women's rights movement.

"The segregated South was defeated by a social protest movement from below—the African American Civil Rights Movement—and by judicial and legislative intervention from outside—the federal government....Southern African Americans, during the years between 1955 and 1965, won the culture wars with southern whites. Civil rights protesters were nonviolent; they were peaceful and studious; and they affirmed American constitutional, democratic, and religious goals...The Civil Rights Movement not only out-sang and out-prayed its opponents, it out-thought them....After 1965, white southerners increasingly won the culture wars in the nation at large. They targeted the enemy not crudely and overtly as black, but as violent, criminal, and immoral, and as leeches on the welfare state at the expense of taxpaying, responsible citizens."

The widespread white acceptance of desegregation efforts in the South in the 1960s and 1970s

nativist views of European immigrants in the mid-1800s.

"I want to speak to you first tonight about a subject even more serious than energy or inflation. I want to talk to you right now about a fundamental threat to American democracy. I do not mean our political and civil liberties. They will endure. The moral judgment of 'good citizen' took on new gender-specific meaning in wartime. Loyal male citizens were defined in productivist ways, 'serving their country' by laboring in the military or . . . defense industries. Loyal female citizens were defined in consumerist ways, as keepers of the home front fires through their own disciplined, patriotic market behavior as well as through the enforcement of high moral standards in others."  
Which of the following would most likely support the ideas described in the excerpt?
a. President Roosevelt's issue of Executive Order 8802 prohibiting workplace discrimination
b. Campaigns to promote women's employment in wartime defense factories
c. The navy's campaign to recruit women to join the WAVES
d. Posters featuring housewives promoting rationing and recycling
Posters featuring housewives promoting rationing and recycling

"We are all in it together. This is a war. We take a few shots and it will be over. We will give them a few shots and it will be over. Don't worry. If we had had a very close election and they were playing the other side I would understand this. Transcript of President Nixon speaking to John Dean in the Oval Office, September 5,1972
U.S. Congress, House. National Archives.
