"The segregated South was defeated by a social protest movement from below—the African American Civil Rights Movement—and by judicial and legislative intervention from outside—the federal government....Southern African Americans, during the years between 1955 and 1965, won the culture wars with southern whites. Civil rights protesters were nonviolent; they were peaceful and studious; and they affirmed American constitutional, democratic, and religious goals...The Civil Rights Movement not only out-sang and out-prayed its opponents, it out-thought them....After 1965, white southerners increasingly won the culture wars in the nation at large. They targeted the enemy not crudely and overtly as black, but as violent, criminal, and immoral, and as leeches on the welfare state at the expense of taxpaying, responsible citizens."
Anthony J. Badger, "Different Perspectives on the Civil Rights Movement"
Reprinted by permission

President Jimmy Carter, "Energy and National Goals," televised address to the nation, July 1979

Two American heroes awarded Medal of Honor during State of the Union
opened.information:
Source: https://www.army.mil/article/290719/two_american_heroes_awarded_medal_of_honor_during_state_of_the_union
Title: Two American heroes awarded Medal of Honor during State of the Union
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
WASHINGTON — On the night of Feb. 24, in the nation's capital, two heroic Americans were honored with the country's highest military decoration, the Medal of Honor.
At the conclusion of his State of the Union address, President Donald J. Trump announced that Army Chief Warrant Officer 5 Eric Slover and retired Navy Capt. Royce Williams were both medal recipients.
Slover, still on active duty, earned the medal for actions last month in Venezuela, while Williams — now 100 years old — received the medal for actions during the Korean War in 1952.
In early January, Trump announced the capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, following a successful overnight joint U.S. military mission in Venezuela's capital of Caracas.
Both Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores de Maduro, were captured by U.S. military forces during that raid, and the two are facing criminal court proceedings tied to a 2020 indictment from the Justice Department on multiple federal charges, including narco-terrorism and drug trafficking.
Slover was part of the military effort to capture Maduro during that raid Jan. 2, Trump said. He was responsible for planning a helicopter mission involving a CH-47 Chinook.
"Slover planned a mission and was the flight lead in the cockpit of the first helicopter," Trump said. "Eric steered the Chinook under the cover of night and descended swiftly upon Maduro's heavily protected military fortress."
The area, Trump said, was heavily guarded by thousands of soldiers.
"While preparing to land, enemy machine guns fired from every angle, and Eric was hit very badly in the leg and hip — one bullet after another," Trump said. "He absorbed four agonizing shots, shredding his leg into numerous pieces."
Despite those injuries, Trump said, Slover pressed on to deliver commandos to the drop zone, where the mission could be carried out.
"[Delivering] the many commandos who would capture and detain Maduro was the only thing Eric was thinking about then," the president said.
"Even as he was gushing blood ... Eric maneuvered his helicopter with all of those lives and souls to face the enemy and let his gunners eliminate the threat — turn the helicopter around so the gunners could take care of business — saving the lives of his fellow warriors from what could have been a catastrophic crash, deep in enemy territory."

After safely landing the helicopter in the right location so the mission could continue, Eric told his copilot, also wounded, to take over.
"The success of the entire mission and the lives of his fellow warriors hinged on Eric's ability to take searing pain," Trump added.
During the State of the Union address, Army Lt. Gen. Jonathan Braga, commander of the Joint Special Operations Command, put the medal around Slover's neck.
The president said there would be a separate event, at the White House, where he would present the medal to Slover.
Nearly 75 years in the making, retired Navy Capt. Royce Williams was also awarded the Medal of Honor. Williams served in World War II, the Korean War and the Vietnam War, the president said. His combat actions in Korea earned him the Medal of Honor.
"In the skies over Korea in 1952, Royce was in the dog fight of a lifetime — a legendary dog fight," Trump said. "Flying through blizzard conditions, his squadron was ambushed by seven Soviet fighter planes. It was his first aerial combat of the war. And despite being massively outnumbered and outgunned, Royce led the takedown of four enemy jets and almost destroyed the others — vanquishing his adversaries while taking 263 bullets to his own plane and being seriously hurt."
For over 50 years, the president said, that mission had been kept secret — Williams didn’t even tell his wife.
"But the legend grew and grew," Trump said. "But tonight, at 100 years old, this brave Navy captain is finally getting the recognition he deserves. He was a legend long before this evening."
First Lady Melania Trump placed the Medal of Honor around Williams' neck.
The president also honored other military heroes during the address. Among those were Coast Guard Petty Officer 2nd Class Scott Ruskan, a rescue swimmer, who was awarded the Legion of Merit for his rescue efforts during a flood last year in central Texas. Ruskan is credited with saving more than 160 lives.
Additionally, two National Guardsmen were awarded Purple Hearts. Army Spc. Sarah Beckstrom and Air Force Staff Sgt. Andrew Wolfe were shot while on patrol in Washington, Nov. 26, 2025.

Beckstrom died from her injuries just a day later. She was awarded the Purple Heart posthumously, with her parents accepting the medal on her behalf. Wolfe was severely injured but has since recovered. He was present at the Capitol to accept the award.

##### **American Golden Age**
This year, the United States will mark 250 years as a nation, and Trump said the United States is stronger than it has ever been.
"Members of Congress and my fellow Americans, our nation is back, bigger, better, richer and stronger than ever before," he said. "Less than five months from now, our country will celebrate an epic milestone in American history: the 250th anniversary of our glorious American independence."
On July 4, Trump said, the United States will mark two and a half centuries of liberty, triumph, progress and freedom, Trump said, adding the best is yet to come.
"You've seen nothing yet," he added. "We're going to do better and better and better — this is the golden age of America."

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor
Title: Medal of Honor
Chunks: 56,57,58,59
## Authority and privileges
### Privileges and courtesies
The 1917 Medal of Honor Board revoked 911 awards, but only 910 names from the Army's Medal of Honor list,[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMears201853,_55-219) including awards to Mary Edwards Walker, William F. "Buffalo Bill" Cody and the first of two awards issued February 10, 1887, to George W. Mindil, who retained his award issued October 25, 1893. None of the 911 impacted recipients were ordered to return their medals, although on the question of whether the recipients could continue to wear their medals, the Judge Advocate General advised the Medal of Honor Board that the Army was not obligated to police the matter.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-220) Walker continued to wear her medal until her death, although some authors mistakenly claim that the Army sought its return.[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-221) Although some sources claim that President Jimmy Carter formally restored her medal posthumously in 1977,[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-clinic-222) this action was actually taken unilaterally by the Army's Board for Correction of Military Records.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMears2018171-51) The Army Board for Correction of Military Records also restored the Medals of Honor of Buffalo Bill and four other civilian scouts in 1989.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMears2018175-52)

## Authority and privileges
### Privileges and courtesies
*   Sixty-one Canadians who served in the United States Armed Forces earned the Medal of Honor, most during the American Civil War. Since 1900, four Canadians have received the medal.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-cbc-223) The only Canadian-born, naturalized U.S. citizen to receive the medal for heroism during the Vietnam War was Peter C. Lemon.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-vwam-224)
While the governing statute for the Army's Medal of Honor (10 U.S.C.§6241), beginning in 1918, explicitly stated that a recipient must be "an officer or enlisted man of the Army", "distinguish himself conspicuously by gallantry and intrepidity at the risk of his life above and beyond the call of duty", and perform an act of valor "in action involving actual conflict with an enemy",[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-Act_of_July_9,_1918,_40_Stat._870-117) exceptions have been made:

## Authority and privileges
### Privileges and courtesies
*   Charles Lindbergh, 1927, civilian pilot, and U.S. Army Air Corps reserve officer.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-225) Lindbergh's medal was authorized by a special act of Congress, which effectively waived his ineligibility on the grounds of not being on military duty, not performing an act of gallantry, and not being in action (combat) against an enemy.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-Act_of_July_9,_1918,_40_Stat._870-117)[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMears201891-226) Lindbergh's award also violated President Coolidge's executive order prohibiting multiple awards for the same action, as he also received a Distinguished Flying Cross for the same transatlantic flight.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMears201891-226)  
*   Major General (Retired) Adolphus Greely was awarded the medal in 1935, on his 91st birthday, "for his life of splendid public service." The result of a special act of Congress similar to Lindbergh's, Greely's medal citation did not reference any acts of valor.[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-227)  
*   Foreign unknown recipients include five WWI Unknowns: the Belgian Unknown Soldier, the British Unknown Warrior, the French Unknown Soldier, the Italian Unknown Soldier, and the Romanian Unknown Soldier.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-228)  

## Authority and privileges
### Privileges and courtesies
*   U.S. unknown recipients include one each from four wars: World War I,[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-229) World War II,[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-230) Korea,[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-231) and Vietnam.[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-232) The Vietnam Unknown was later identified as Air Force First Lieutenant Michael Blassie through the use of DNA identification.[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-dvidshub.net-233) Blassie's family asked for his Medal of Honor, but the Department of Defense denied the request in 1998.[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-dvidshub.net-233) According to Undersecretary of Defense Rudy de Leon, the medal was awarded symbolically to all Vietnam unknowns, not to Blassie specifically.[[230]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-234) The action also resulted in clarification of unknown medal awards in the FY2005 defense bill, which expressly stated such medals are "awarded to the member as a representative of the members of the armed forces who died in such war or other armed conflict and whose remains have not been identified, and not to the individual personally."[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMears2018116-116)

Indonesia's National Hero titles and the politics of unresolved violence
opened.information:
Source: https://www.lowyinstitute.org/the-interpreter/indonesia-s-national-hero-titles-and-the-politics-of-unresolved-violence
Title: Indonesia’s National Hero titles and the politics of unresolved violence
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
As Indonesia approaches National Heroes Day (_Hari Pahlawan_) on 10 November, the decree naming this year’s National Heroes (_Pahlawan Nasional_) is, a deputy minister says, already on President Prabowo Subianto’s desk (Opens in new window). The title is the republic’s highest honour, awarded posthumously since 1959. Last year’s list, and a campaign to add a murdered journalist to the next one, show what the title does when it goes to victims of the state’s own violence.
Civil society demands the state recognition and accountability for past abuses. Whatever the government intends, the outcome has been consistent. The state grants the title once the criminal accountability is no longer legally possible.
The question is not only domestic. Indonesia chairs the UN Human Rights Council (Opens in new window) in 2026, and the government is drafting a revision (Opens in new window) of the 1999 Human Rights Law that could give the National Commission on Human Rights (Komnas HAM) investigative powers over the gravest cases. Whether a New Order killing can still reach a court is a live question.
On 10 November 2025, Prabowo conferred the title on ten people, including Marsinah, a labour activist killed in 1993. When asked whether her murder investigation would now be reopened, State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi replied that the two matters were unconnected (Opens in new window): “Let us look forward together. Every generation has its time, every era has its people, its achievements, its strengths, its shortcomings.”
> What is new in the cases from Suharto’s military-backed New Order is how the honour interacts with the clock of criminal procedure.
This not unprecedented, in 1963 Sukarno, Indonesia’s first president, conferred the title (Opens in new window) on Tan Malaka, a revolutionary executed by Republican troops in 1949. What is new in the cases from Suharto’s military-backed New Order (1966 to 1998) is how the honour interacts with the clock of criminal procedure.

The case of Marsinah perfectly illustrates this paradox. In May 1993 Marsinah, a 24-year-old worker at a watch factory in East Java, disappeared after a strike. Under the New Order the army policed labour disputes, and she went to the local military command to ask after colleagues interrogated there. Days later her body, bearing signs of torture, was found in a forest hut. The factory owner and several employees were convicted in 1994; the Supreme Court acquitted them all in 1995 (Opens in new window). No one has been charged since.
Her nomination came from below. Nganjuk, her home district, began the nomination in 2022 (Opens in new window), and on May Day 2025 Prabowo, a retired general and former son-in-law of Suharto, pledged his support (Opens in new window) on condition that union leaders agreed. The resulting decree formalised a stark historical irony. The decree that named her also named Suharto, under whose regime she was killed.
Anis Hidayah, who chairs Komnas HAM, the body that decides whether a case counts as a gross human rights violation eligible for a special court, welcomed the recognition while naming the paradox (Opens in new window): “The person is given a title, yet the case itself remains unresolved.”
Prabowo publicly admitted the structural violence behind her death. Opening a Marsinah museum on 16 May 2026, Prabowo said (Opens in new window): “I have only just realised and understood that collusion by security personnel was used by certain capitalists, and this is a culture we must not continue.”
The family of the late Marsinah, the labour activist murdered during former President Suharto's leadership, during a ceremony with President Prabowo Subianto held to mark the National Heroes Day at the State Palace in Jakarta, 10 November 2025 (Bay Ismoyo/AFP via Getty Images)

Under the old Criminal Code, in force until January 2026, prosecution for murder lapsed after 18 years, so Marsinah’s case expired in 2011. Only reclassification as a gross human rights violation, which carries no time bar, could reopen it. On 5 May 2026 a committee marking 33 years since her death went to Komnas HAM to demand that (Opens in new window). The commission refused and treats the killing as an ordinary crime, while claiming to have lost its 2013 investigation file.
A second New Order killing is now following the same dynamic. Journalists’ associations in Yogyakarta are nominating Fuad Muhammad Syafruddin, known as Udin, a reporter for the daily _Bernas_ who was beaten to death in August 1996 (Opens in new window) after reporting on corruption in Bantul district. Police framed a local driver with a confession (Opens in new window) bought with alcohol and money; a court acquitted him in 1997.
A senior Supreme Court justice argued in 2013 (Opens in new window) that the case could not lapse because the real killers had never been tried; police treated it as time-barred (Opens in new window) from August 2014.
With prosecution foreclosed, the press groups turned to the honours system. On 29 October 2026 Deputy Minister of Social Affairs Agus Jabo Priyono backed Udin’s candidacy (Opens in new window) for a later cycle; this year’s is closed. Should Udin be inducted, his widow would qualify under a 2018 presidential regulation (Opens in new window) (which, naming only spouses and children, appears to exclude Marsinah’s sisters) for a family allowance of 50 million rupiah (about US$2,800) a year.

Indonesia’s 2009 Law on Titles (Opens in new window) assesses a candidate’s service and example, remaining legally blind to the circumstances of death or the evasion of justice. By the time unions and press groups push a victim of New Order violence through district, provincial and ministerial review to the Council on Titles, the criminal calendar has run out. The state does not use the hero title to close the criminal file. It safely confers the title once the file is already closed. Whether that remains the only outcome depends less on the honours system than on what the revised Human Rights Law gives Komnas HAM, and whether a commission that that routinely “loses” its own investigation files is capable of enforcing them.

## [PDF page 1]
Jamaican Honours and Awards System  
The National Honours and Awards Act, promulgated on the 18th of July 1969, made it  
possible for the nation to recognize those who, by their service and contribution, have had a  
meaningful and significant impact on national life.
National Honours and Awards are administered by the Chancery of the Orders of the  
Societies of Honour in the Office of the Prime Minister.
Formal recognition of service to Jamaica and its citizens may be given by the conferment of  
the Honour of one of the Orders of the six Societies of Honour established under the  
provisions of the National Honours and Awards Act, namely:  
•  The Order of National Hero  
•  The Order of the Nation (ON)  
•  The Order of Excellence (OE)  
•  The Order of Merit (OM)  
•  The Order of Jamaica (OJ)  
•  The Order of Distinction  
o  Commander Class (CD)  
o  Officer Class (OD)  
and by the award of  
•  Badge of Honour for Gallantry [BH(G)]  
•  Badge of Honour for Meritorious Service[BH(M)]  
•  Badge of Honour for Long and Faithful Service  [BH(L)]  
and  
•  Medal of Honour for Gallantry  
•  Medal of Honour for Meritorious Service  
•  Medal of Honour for Long and Faithful Service  
•  Medal of Honour for Efficient Service
Description of Jamaican Honours and Awards
Order of National Hero  
The Order of National Hero is the most senior Order. The honour of  
the Order of National Hero may be conferred upon any person who  
was born in Jamaica or is, or at the time of his or her death was, a  
citizen of Jamaica and rendered to Jamaica service of a most  
distinguished nature. A member of the Order is entitled to be styled  
“Right Excellent” (which may be abbreviated to Rt. Excellent) and the  
motto of the Order is “He built a city which hath foundations”.

## [PDF page 1]
The insignia of the Order of National Hero consists of a gold and  
white enamelled star of fourteen points, the centre of which shows the  
heraldic Arms of Jamaica in gold on a black enamelled medallion.  
This is surrounded by the motto of the Order in gold lettering on green enamel. The collar  
badge is suspended from a black, gold and green neck riband by a gold and green enamelled  
laurel wreath.

## [PDF page 2]
Order of the Nation  
The honour of the Order of the Nation (ON), the second most senior  
Order, may be conferred upon any Governor-General of Jamaica and  
upon any person who has been appointed as Prime Minister of  
Jamaica, not being a person upon whom the honour of the Order of  
National Hero has been conferred. Members of the Order are styled  
"the Most Honourable” and the spouse of the member is also entitled  
to be so styled. Members of the Order are entitled to place the letters  
“ON” after their name. The motto of the Order is "One Nation under  
God".
The insignia of the Order of the Nation consists of a magnificent  
breast star bearing the heraldic Arms of Jamaica on a red enamelled background in the centre  
and surrounded by the motto of the Order in gold lettering on green enamel. Between the  
points of the star are gold representations of pineapples. The broad watered silk sash is in a  
brilliant red with narrow green edging.
Order of Excellence  
The honour of the Order of Excellence (OE) is ranked equally, in the  
order of precedence, with the honour of the Order of the Nation and  
may be conferred upon any foreign Head of State or foreign Head of  
Government, and upon any foreign former Head of State or foreign  
former Head of Government. Members of the Order are styled "The  
Most Honourable" and are entitled to place the letters “OE” after their

WASHINGTON — On the night of Feb. 24, in the nation's capital, two heroic Americans were honored with the country's highest military decoration, the Medal of Honor.
At the conclusion of his State of the Union address, President Donald J. Trump announced that Army Chief Warrant Officer 5 Eric Slover and retired Navy Capt. Royce Williams were both medal recipients.
Slover, still on active duty, earned the medal for actions last month in Venezuela, while Williams — now 100 years old — received the medal for actions during the Korean War in 1952.
In early January, Trump announced the capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, following a successful overnight joint U.S. military mission in Venezuela's capital of Caracas.
Both Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores de Maduro, were captured by U.S. military forces during that raid, and the two are facing criminal court proceedings tied to a 2020 indictment from the Justice Department on multiple federal charges, including narco-terrorism and drug trafficking.
Slover was part of the military effort to capture Maduro during that raid Jan. 2, Trump said. He was responsible for planning a helicopter mission involving a CH-47 Chinook.
"Slover planned a mission and was the flight lead in the cockpit of the first helicopter," Trump said. "Eric steered the Chinook under the cover of night and descended swiftly upon Maduro's heavily protected military fortress."
The area, Trump said, was heavily guarded by thousands of soldiers.
"While preparing to land, enemy machine guns fired from every angle, and Eric was hit very badly in the leg and hip — one bullet after another," Trump said. "He absorbed four agonizing shots, shredding his leg into numerous pieces."
Despite those injuries, Trump said, Slover pressed on to deliver commandos to the drop zone, where the mission could be carried out.
"[Delivering] the many commandos who would capture and detain Maduro was the only thing Eric was thinking about then," the president said.
"Even as he was gushing blood ... Eric maneuvered his helicopter with all of those lives and souls to face the enemy and let his gunners eliminate the threat — turn the helicopter around so the gunners could take care of business — saving the lives of his fellow warriors from what could have been a catastrophic crash, deep in enemy territory."
texts.1:
After safely landing the helicopter in the right location so the mission could continue, Eric told his copilot, also wounded, to take over.
"The success of the entire mission and the lives of his fellow warriors hinged on Eric's ability to take searing pain," Trump added.
During the State of the Union address, Army Lt. Gen. Jonathan Braga, commander of the Joint Special Operations Command, put the medal around Slover's neck.
The president said there would be a separate event, at the White House, where he would present the medal to Slover.
Nearly 75 years in the making, retired Navy Capt. Royce Williams was also awarded the Medal of Honor. Williams served in World War II, the Korean War and the Vietnam War, the president said. His combat actions in Korea earned him the Medal of Honor.
"In the skies over Korea in 1952, Royce was in the dog fight of a lifetime — a legendary dog fight," Trump said. "Flying through blizzard conditions, his squadron was ambushed by seven Soviet fighter planes. It was his first aerial combat of the war. And despite being massively outnumbered and outgunned, Royce led the takedown of four enemy jets and almost destroyed the others — vanquishing his adversaries while taking 263 bullets to his own plane and being seriously hurt."
For over 50 years, the president said, that mission had been kept secret — Williams didn’t even tell his wife.
"But the legend grew and grew," Trump said. "But tonight, at 100 years old, this brave Navy captain is finally getting the recognition he deserves. He was a legend long before this evening."
First Lady Melania Trump placed the Medal of Honor around Williams' neck.
The president also honored other military heroes during the address. Among those were Coast Guard Petty Officer 2nd Class Scott Ruskan, a rescue swimmer, who was awarded the Legion of Merit for his rescue efforts during a flood last year in central Texas. Ruskan is credited with saving more than 160 lives.
Additionally, two National Guardsmen were awarded Purple Hearts. Army Spc. Sarah Beckstrom and Air Force Staff Sgt. Andrew Wolfe were shot while on patrol in Washington, Nov. 26, 2025.
texts.2: Beckstrom died from her injuries just a day later. She was awarded the Purple Heart posthumously, with her parents accepting the medal on her behalf. Wolfe was severely injured but has since recovered. He was present at the Capitol to accept the award.
texts.3:
##### **American Golden Age**
This year, the United States will mark 250 years as a nation, and Trump said the United States is stronger than it has ever been.
"Members of Congress and my fellow Americans, our nation is back, bigger, better, richer and stronger than ever before," he said. "Less than five months from now, our country will celebrate an epic milestone in American history: the 250th anniversary of our glorious American independence."
On July 4, Trump said, the United States will mark two and a half centuries of liberty, triumph, progress and freedom, Trump said, adding the best is yet to come.
"You've seen nothing yet," he added. "We're going to do better and better and better — this is the golden age of America."

As Indonesia approaches National Heroes Day (_Hari Pahlawan_) on 10 November, the decree naming this year’s National Heroes (_Pahlawan Nasional_) is, a deputy minister says, already on President Prabowo Subianto’s desk (Opens in new window). The title is the republic’s highest honour, awarded posthumously since 1959. Last year’s list, and a campaign to add a murdered journalist to the next one, show what the title does when it goes to victims of the state’s own violence.
Civil society demands the state recognition and accountability for past abuses. Whatever the government intends, the outcome has been consistent. The state grants the title once the criminal accountability is no longer legally possible.
The question is not only domestic. Indonesia chairs the UN Human Rights Council (Opens in new window) in 2026, and the government is drafting a revision (Opens in new window) of the 1999 Human Rights Law that could give the National Commission on Human Rights (Komnas HAM) investigative powers over the gravest cases. Whether a New Order killing can still reach a court is a live question.
On 10 November 2025, Prabowo conferred the title on ten people, including Marsinah, a labour activist killed in 1993. When asked whether her murder investigation would now be reopened, State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi replied that the two matters were unconnected (Opens in new window): “Let us look forward together. Every generation has its time, every era has its people, its achievements, its strengths, its shortcomings.”
> What is new in the cases from Suharto’s military-backed New Order is how the honour interacts with the clock of criminal procedure.
This not unprecedented, in 1963 Sukarno, Indonesia’s first president, conferred the title (Opens in new window) on Tan Malaka, a revolutionary executed by Republican troops in 1949. What is new in the cases from Suharto’s military-backed New Order (1966 to 1998) is how the honour interacts with the clock of criminal procedure.
texts.1:
The case of Marsinah perfectly illustrates this paradox. In May 1993 Marsinah, a 24-year-old worker at a watch factory in East Java, disappeared after a strike. Under the New Order the army policed labour disputes, and she went to the local military command to ask after colleagues interrogated there. Days later her body, bearing signs of torture, was found in a forest hut. The factory owner and several employees were convicted in 1994; the Supreme Court acquitted them all in 1995 (Opens in new window). No one has been charged since.
Her nomination came from below. Nganjuk, her home district, began the nomination in 2022 (Opens in new window), and on May Day 2025 Prabowo, a retired general and former son-in-law of Suharto, pledged his support (Opens in new window) on condition that union leaders agreed. The resulting decree formalised a stark historical irony. The decree that named her also named Suharto, under whose regime she was killed.
Anis Hidayah, who chairs Komnas HAM, the body that decides whether a case counts as a gross human rights violation eligible for a special court, welcomed the recognition while naming the paradox (Opens in new window): “The person is given a title, yet the case itself remains unresolved.”
Prabowo publicly admitted the structural violence behind her death. Opening a Marsinah museum on 16 May 2026, Prabowo said (Opens in new window): “I have only just realised and understood that collusion by security personnel was used by certain capitalists, and this is a culture we must not continue.”
The family of the late Marsinah, the labour activist murdered during former President Suharto's leadership, during a ceremony with President Prabowo Subianto held to mark the National Heroes Day at the State Palace in Jakarta, 10 November 2025 (Bay Ismoyo/AFP via Getty Images)
texts.2:
Under the old Criminal Code, in force until January 2026, prosecution for murder lapsed after 18 years, so Marsinah’s case expired in 2011. Only reclassification as a gross human rights violation, which carries no time bar, could reopen it. On 5 May 2026 a committee marking 33 years since her death went to Komnas HAM to demand that (Opens in new window). The commission refused and treats the killing as an ordinary crime, while claiming to have lost its 2013 investigation file.
A second New Order killing is now following the same dynamic. Journalists’ associations in Yogyakarta are nominating Fuad Muhammad Syafruddin, known as Udin, a reporter for the daily _Bernas_ who was beaten to death in August 1996 (Opens in new window) after reporting on corruption in Bantul district. Police framed a local driver with a confession (Opens in new window) bought with alcohol and money; a court acquitted him in 1997.
A senior Supreme Court justice argued in 2013 (Opens in new window) that the case could not lapse because the real killers had never been tried; police treated it as time-barred (Opens in new window) from August 2014.
With prosecution foreclosed, the press groups turned to the honours system. On 29 October 2026 Deputy Minister of Social Affairs Agus Jabo Priyono backed Udin’s candidacy (Opens in new window) for a later cycle; this year’s is closed. Should Udin be inducted, his widow would qualify under a 2018 presidential regulation (Opens in new window) (which, naming only spouses and children, appears to exclude Marsinah’s sisters) for a family allowance of 50 million rupiah (about US$2,800) a year.
texts.3: Indonesia’s 2009 Law on Titles (Opens in new window) assesses a candidate’s service and example, remaining legally blind to the circumstances of death or the evasion of justice. By the time unions and press groups push a victim of New Order violence through district, provincial and ministerial review to the Council on Titles, the criminal calendar has run out. The state does not use the hero title to close the criminal file. It safely confers the title once the file is already closed. Whether that remains the only outcome depends less on the honours system than on what the revised Human Rights Law gives Komnas HAM, and whether a commission that that routinely “loses” its own investigation files is capable of enforcing them.

Jamaican Honours and Awards System  
The National Honours and Awards Act, promulgated on the 18th of July 1969, made it  
possible for the nation to recognize those who, by their service and contribution, have had a  
meaningful and significant impact on national life.
National Honours and Awards are administered by the Chancery of the Orders of the  
Societies of Honour in the Office of the Prime Minister.
Formal recognition of service to Jamaica and its citizens may be given by the conferment of  
the Honour of one of the Orders of the six Societies of Honour established under the  
provisions of the National Honours and Awards Act, namely:  
•  The Order of National Hero  
•  The Order of the Nation (ON)  
•  The Order of Excellence (OE)  
•  The Order of Merit (OM)  
•  The Order of Jamaica (OJ)  
•  The Order of Distinction  
o  Commander Class (CD)

and by the award of

and  
•  Medal of Honour for Gallantry

distinguished nature. A member of the Order is entitled to be styled  
“Right Excellent” (which may be abbreviated to Rt. Excellent) and the  
motto of the Order is “He built a city which hath foundations”.

## Authority and privileges
### Privileges and courtesies
The 1917 Medal of Honor Board revoked 911 awards, but only 910 names from the Army's Medal of Honor list,[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMears201853,_55-219) including awards to Mary Edwards Walker, William F. "Buffalo Bill" Cody and the first of two awards issued February 10, 1887, to George W. Mindil, who retained his award issued October 25, 1893. None of the 911 impacted recipients were ordered to return their medals, although on the question of whether the recipients could continue to wear their medals, the Judge Advocate General advised the Medal of Honor Board that the Army was not obligated to police the matter.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-220) Walker continued to wear her medal until her death, although some authors mistakenly claim that the Army sought its return.[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-221) Although some sources claim that President Jimmy Carter formally restored her medal posthumously in 1977,[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-clinic-222) this action was actually taken unilaterally by the Army's Board for Correction of Military Records.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMears2018171-51) The Army Board for Correction of Military Records also restored the Medals of Honor of Buffalo Bill and four other civilian scouts in 1989.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMears2018175-52)
texts.57:
## Authority and privileges
### Privileges and courtesies
*   Sixty-one Canadians who served in the United States Armed Forces earned the Medal of Honor, most during the American Civil War. Since 1900, four Canadians have received the medal.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-cbc-223) The only Canadian-born, naturalized U.S. citizen to receive the medal for heroism during the Vietnam War was Peter C. Lemon.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-vwam-224)
While the governing statute for the Army's Medal of Honor (10 U.S.C.§6241), beginning in 1918, explicitly stated that a recipient must be "an officer or enlisted man of the Army", "distinguish himself conspicuously by gallantry and intrepidity at the risk of his life above and beyond the call of duty", and perform an act of valor "in action involving actual conflict with an enemy",[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-Act_of_July_9,_1918,_40_Stat._870-117) exceptions have been made:
texts.58:
## Authority and privileges
### Privileges and courtesies
*   Charles Lindbergh, 1927, civilian pilot, and U.S. Army Air Corps reserve officer.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-225) Lindbergh's medal was authorized by a special act of Congress, which effectively waived his ineligibility on the grounds of not being on military duty, not performing an act of gallantry, and not being in action (combat) against an enemy.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-Act_of_July_9,_1918,_40_Stat._870-117)[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMears201891-226) Lindbergh's award also violated President Coolidge's executive order prohibiting multiple awards for the same action, as he also received a Distinguished Flying Cross for the same transatlantic flight.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMears201891-226)  
*   Major General (Retired) Adolphus Greely was awarded the medal in 1935, on his 91st birthday, "for his life of splendid public service." The result of a special act of Congress similar to Lindbergh's, Greely's medal citation did not reference any acts of valor.[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-227)  
*   Foreign unknown recipients include five WWI Unknowns: the Belgian Unknown Soldier, the British Unknown Warrior, the French Unknown Soldier, the Italian Unknown Soldier, and the Romanian Unknown Soldier.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-228)
texts.59:
## Authority and privileges
### Privileges and courtesies
*   U.S. unknown recipients include one each from four wars: World War I,[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-229) World War II,[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-230) Korea,[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-231) and Vietnam.[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-232) The Vietnam Unknown was later identified as Air Force First Lieutenant Michael Blassie through the use of DNA identification.[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-dvidshub.net-233) Blassie's family asked for his Medal of Honor, but the Department of Defense denied the request in 1998.[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-dvidshub.net-233) According to Undersecretary of Defense Rudy de Leon, the medal was awarded symbolically to all Vietnam unknowns, not to Blassie specifically.[[230]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-234) The action also resulted in clarification of unknown medal awards in the FY2005 defense bill, which expressly stated such medals are "awarded to the member as a representative of the members of the armed forces who died in such war or other armed conflict and whose remains have not been identified, and not to the individual personally."[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMears2018116-116)

Title: A Conversation With Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre of Norway and President Alexander Stubb of Finland | Council on Foreign Relations
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,15,16,17,18,19,20,21,22
Highlights of the interview were broadcast on CNN’s _Fareed Zakaria GPS_ on Sunday, September 27 at 10:00 a.m. (EDT), with a planned replay at 1:00 p.m. (EDT).
ZAKARIA: All right. I’d like to welcome all of you. We have, of course, very distinguished guests with us today—the Prime Minister of Norway, the president of Finland.
This is called the Russell Leffingwell Lecture. And we do want to thank the Leffingwell family for their generosity in endowing this lecture, especially Tom and Ted Leffingwell Pulling. Appreciate it greatly. Russell Leffingwell was a charter member of the CFR who also served as its president from 1944 to ’46, and its chairman from ’46 to ’53.
You know the usual rules for the Council apply. We will begin with a conversation, and then about halfway through I’ll open it up to questions.
Welcome—I can’t say presidents, I can’t say prime ministers, so I’m going to say Your Excellencies. (Laughter.) Let’s start with the issue that really must be preoccupying you from a national security point of view, which is the war in Ukraine. It doesn’t seem like much is changing on the battlefield. There are some indications that—recently that actually the Ukrainians have been doing well. On the other hand, the Russians have been able to destroy much of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. And they have these jet Shaheds that seem to be able to go faster and evade the Ukrainian efforts to intercept. How would you read the battlefront, to begin with?
STUBB: Well, I think there’s good news and bad news. The good news is that Ukraine is doing better politically, militarily, and financially than they have been doing at any time this year. I’d argue that they’ve been on top ever since December. On the battlefield, this means that the killing ratio is about one to five, one Ukrainian for five Russians. It means that since January Russia has advanced only 900 square kilometers, and Ukraine has taken back 800 square kilometers. It means that Ukraine is able to hit long-range targets, in terms of oil refineries and logistical centers. This is all good news. So it’s pretty much a stalemate.

The bad news, of course, is that winter is coming. And Ukraine right now desperately needs three things. One is air defense because, the ballistic missiles are coming through. Two is energy installments. And three is finances. So, you know, we’re working both to support Ukraine as best we can, together with Jonas and many others, and then on top of that we try to work with the peace negotiations as well.
ZAKARIA: Prime Minister, the big strategic reality that Ukraine faces economically has been the collapse of American support. American military assistance is essentially down to zero. The Europeans have stepped up extraordinarily, but now Ukraine says it has a $27 billion deficit. And it’s quite possible that this will get worse because, I was just in Ukraine, and the industrial economy has essentially shut down because of the—because of what President Stubb was saying. The energy infrastructure has been damaged badly enough that very few factories, big factories, are running. Do you think Europe will be able to do what it takes to support Ukraine?
STORE: Well, part of that finance is becoming more and more Northern European. I think that the Northern Europeans have stood, you know, the course until now. I think that the way Ukraine is resisting is telling us the following, how do wars end? They end when the warring parties see that, you know, the war is not going to deliver what they went into this, and the pain of the war is going to exceed what you can benefit from the war. I sense that we are getting closer to that point, in the sense that it’s a war that obviously should have not started. Every purpose that was defined when it started has not been achieved, basically. And now we’re five years into it soon, and it should stop.

So I think, yes, it will be critical during this winter. But I think, you know, the Ukrainians have shown us again and again their will to resist this. They are not going to lay down. The Donbas scenario, where President Putin, you know, he wants Donbas. There are 200,000 people living there. And Ukraine controls this area. And they will not give it up. They cannot give it up. It will be against their constitution. And no Ukrainian leader can give up a territory with people that they have died for. So that will not happen. So, you know, does that mean that we will approach a moment—and I think the president and I have, you know, been old colleagues in in foreign policy for almost twenty years now. We see that that moment must approach.
And that’s why I think the U.S., although, you know, I regret that there is not financial support. I think, you know, that’s a mistake. But they are critically important to get the diplomacy moving. So we need focus, and we will spend some time this week, I think, to make that voice heard. You know, to have an American role in that diplomacy to get it going. And then it will be our responsibility to see to it that Europe, which will have to live with the aftermath of this conflict. This is a conflict in our territory. Russia is our neighbor. That we can define a security structure for the future. But that moment has to come sooner than later, that there is a start of the end of this war.
ZAKARIA: President Stubb, you are sometimes called a Trump whisperer for the Europeans. You do have a good personal relationship with him. You talk to the negotiators often. Do you get the sense that there is any real movement on the negotiation side? Again, when I was in Kyiv the feeling was they were being—they were being given the same old offers, that there was no real progress.

STUBB: Well, I think, Jonas and I were there, I think, a week before you. And I think the mood then was rather positive. And we had spoken to the American negotiators a few times before they went in and right after they came out. And we spoke to president Zelensky, was it a week ago, a week and a half ago in in Oslo, and we’ll see him here this week. I think the fact that Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff went to Moscow, that John Ratcliffe went to Moscow, that was significant. And then that the two negotiators went to Kyiv got the ball rolling.
Now, my feeling is that out of those early negotiations there’s now sentiment that the Anchorage deal is out of the window, so three plus two doesn’t exist anymore.
ZAKARIA: Just explain what that is.
STUBB: And that means that the Russians wanted to take three of the oblasts and leave two to the Ukrainians. And this was their sort of assumption of the deal in Alaska. And this is out of the window. As is Ukrainian neutrality. And I think they are going to get back to so-called trilateral negotiations—Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S.—on a lower level, trying to get perhaps a partial deal, which would have to do something with the Black Sea, with grain corridors, and energy corridors. So my sense is that things are moving. Does this mean that we’re going to get peace immediately? No. But there has to come a point when, you know, the Russians realize that enough is enough and they will not have achieved their goals, which was to basically take over Ukraine, deny its independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity.

ZAKARIA: Alex, you’ve been—President Stubb, you’ve been a serious scholar of international relations. You’re now a serious player. What is the most surprising thing that you found, going from being a scholar to a practitioner?
STUBB: Well, I always had this sort of E.H. Carr type of an idea, that I had a dream when I was young or came out of Furman University, my alma mater, in 1993, that I would be able to oscillate between the world of academia and the world of politics, or actually at the time civil service. Politics came quite late, in 2004. And I don’t think I’ve been surprised by anything except how much more I get out of taking time in one domain and coming back. So, for instance, I mean, I left politics permanently in in 2016. And I fully admit, I would not sit here had not, you know, Russia attacked Ukraine in 2022. I was always a NATO advocate, and then I was asked to run for president. And I thought, OK, I’ll do it.
But I had four years in academia, you know, writing my book and thinking about big concepts. And then coming back into a situation where you feel that you have curveballs coming at you every day at the pace of a fastball. And then to be able to conceptualize things and categorize things has helped me immensely. And the final point, I think in this job if you don’t read books and if you don’t write, you only get into this sort of churning process. And I think it would be very difficult for me to cope with it. So I just need to stop and do my reading, you know, either on a plane, or early morning, or whenever it is. So I’m just very fortunate that I’ve been able to go back and forth between academia and practice.
STORE: Can I say that I welcome him back to politics? (Laughter.) So—
ZAKARIA: And I hope you will share that advice to read with some other world leaders. (Laughter.)
STUBB: Oh, he reads a lot.
ZAKARIA: (Laughs.) Mike Froman.
Q: Well, first of all, thank you both for being here. Thank you, Fareed, for moderating this.

Mr. President, you mentioned the importance of middle powers. Mr. Prime Minister, you’ve just come from Canada, talking with Prime Minister Carney, the recent proponent of the role of middle powers. What, in reality, do you think the prospects and the limitations are for middle powers to play a central role in the world going forward, without the United States involvement or leadership?
STUBB: Well, I think Jonas and I don’t consider ourselves to be middle powers. Perhaps Norway, but not Finland. (Laughter.) No. So, you know, we talk about ourselves being in the back office. So if foreign policy is about values, interest, and power, we have values and interest. And the way in which we project power is through sharing information and being in the back office and helping out. But I would consider myself to be more of an institutionalist than a middle power kind of guy. I know we live in a middle power world, where you have these unholy coalitions and alliances coming up. And they, you know, have an impact. But I still believe that regional integration is the best way for a small country to work. Middle powers are probably not going to gain that much traction with the big powers, who want to only play the power game with the bigger countries. So China, the U.S., India. That’s why I think trying to get things into an institutional framework is probably more effective for small guys like us.
STORE: I agree with that. And then I think, you know, there’s a particular moment now where there is an opportunity for pragmatism. What can work? And where are there opportunities that you, without prestige, can go in and say, you know, if we put this together it may work. And here, I think, you know, again, like-minded countries—as I said, the president and I, we come from different parties, but I think we share this kind of.
STUBB: I’m independent. (Laughter.)

STORE: You were elected on the bill. (Laughter.) No, but the point here is that—and here and here I see also, you know, the Mark Carney appeal. I mean, he’s in in a very special situation with this—you know, this U.S. tension which is there. But it is also going after what can work in this world, where kind of the news is that more and more is not working. And that’s creating, you know, a certain also idea of potential optimism, that we can get things to work. On trade for example, we see that trade is breaking down in the sense that tariffs are coming in again. I think it is a very bad idea. It is hurting all parties. But 70 to 80 percent of world trade is still according to the rules.
So how do we work with WTO to reform it and make it, you know, sustain? How do we make the international cooperation that works and deliver results, make them vibrant? And here I think the Arctic, you know, it is an area of pragmatism that we look after. So here countries, like ours, and I wouldn’t call us middle powers either, but, you know, pragmatic countries that have open economies, highly digitalized. We don’t invent much AI, but we are probably the ones who use them most, and, you know, can spread it to a population where the level of education can take it on board. So we are active and engaged.
STUBB: Can I steal one of Jonas’ examples that he gave already, I think, when we were foreign minister way back in the Stone Ages. And it’s linked to middle powers. If you put the five Nordic countries together, we would be G-10. So that—you know, if we’re together, that kind of gives us a middle power status. And I think that’s very much in our DNA.
ZAKARIA: Ma’am, in the blue, yeah.
Q: Michelle Caruso-Cabrera, longtime journalist. Thanks so much for doing this.

Prime Minister, the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund does not invest in private equity, despite its large size. I’m sure that breaks the hearts of many people here in the audience. (Laughter.) Even as the number of publicly traded stocks in the world get smaller and smaller. Just this past week, the fund asked if it could invest in private equity, and yet the answer is no. Do you think that will ever change, and why is that?
STORE: Well, I think, you know, it is by nature, because it’s this kind of fund owned by—it’s a sovereign wealth owned by people. It has a certain risk averse. I wouldn’t exclude that that could not come, because it should look at the—at, you know, what you call the kind of universe of investment, needs to be countries where there where there is a rule of law for the equity markets and so on. It has evolved into investing in infrastructure, which is one big step. There was also a chapter where it invested in in real estate. So I wouldn’t exclude that coming. But, you know, there are quite high demands on control mechanisms, transparency, and how things can be available. But, you know, I wouldn’t exclude. But it’s not for the immediate.
ZAKARIA: Let’s take—follow the good example of the lady who just asked the question, and if you can direct your question to one of the two leaders, it’d be easier. So I think I saw back there. Yes, sir.
Q: Hi, my name is Hall Wang.
I’ll direct my question to the prime minister. So, on top of your country being really good at winning Winter Olympic medals, you’re also a great adopter of electric vehicles. As you know, the electric vehicle industry is becoming increasingly present with Chinese companies like BYD. Do you ever think it’s an intelligent, pragmatic approach to put tariffs on Chinese EVs to potentially protect Western car companies? And also, if you could share your preference for electric vehicles, that’d be fun as well.

STORE: Well, we were early in incentivizing electric vehicles. You know, taking away—we had VAT. And now the fact is that about 98 percent of new car sales in Norway is non-fossil. So that is a major achievement, and it’s helping us to get emissions down, and it is doing the right thing. The number of Chinese cars is going up. It’s up to Norwegians what they want to buy. I think we have a challenge when it comes to government, both local government and central government. Do you buy Russian—do you buy Chinese busses, for example? If you know that there may be intelligence gathering through the bus system, transport system? There are important questions to be asked. And probably the answer can be no.
And then, you know, Norway, we are not producing cars. But when I am in China, I second my European colleagues who say that, you know, there are reasons to challenge and question the way you support your industry, the way you subsidize it not through traditional subsidies but through a whole set of mechanisms very hard to penetrate. And this is building. This conflict is building. For a car-producing country like Germany, it is it is a very, very complex and dramatic issue. And I support European colleagues, you know, taking a firm line on that. I was foreign minister back at the time when China got into WTO. And we thought that was the right thing to do because we would have level playing field and rules to support. But then it has to work both ways. And here there are really, I think, issues that need to be handled.
ZAKARIA: Sir, over there on the aisle, exactly you.
Q: Hi. Jay Markowitz, Regeneron Ventures.

You each commented about playing the long game with ideas. And I would argue that the way to do that is by supporting science and scientists who do it. Now I think is an historic opportunity for other countries to step up and fill some of the gaps, become a more welcoming place and more supportive place to fund that research. I won’t pile on, on the $2.25 trillion opportunity that you have in Norway that you’ve mentioned. You’re investing in—you have invested in the stock market as well as infrastructure. But I’m curious what each of you think of this. You talk about the Nordic region together combined is like the G-10. So what are your thoughts about moving science forward and using that as a way to advance your growth? Thank you.
ZAKARIA: Alex, why don’t you start?
STUBB: Well, I mean, I think it’s the basis of everything. I mean, education is the basis of civilization, research and development and innovation is the basis of the economy. And, of course, right now from the U.S., unfortunately, there’s been a brain drain. And I think a lot of us in Europe are trying to work on, OK, how do we deal with this? I also believe that when it comes to R&D, it’s not only public money. I mean, Finland got out of the—a difficult situation, a banking crisis, in the early 1990s by putting a lot of public investment into R&D. But now when money is scarce, it needs to also come from the private side.

I’m actually extremely bullish about the Finnish economy at the moment, because we have a lot of the, you know, chokepoints or key elements of what it takes to be driven in an AI economy. You know, in terms of networks with Nokia, or in terms of quantum computing with e-companies, or in terms of a satellite industry. But that needs some kind of a cluster. So therefore, we have, for instance, what we call Aalto University in the Helsinki region, which has a lot of incubators and sort of mixes academia, science, and business. And I think this is sort of the interaction that you need in order for you to thrive. And, as an academic, I also think that, you know, it’s quite often in research a system of trial and error. So you try to work on something on a scientific method, and then you fail, and then you try again, and then you fail, and perhaps on a third time you come and get a solution. So this is a type of mentality that I’d like to see us have in Finland when it comes to research and development and education and learning.
ZAKARIA: Prime Minister, you must be asked all the time why don’t you spend your 2.25 trillion (dollars) on X, Y, and Z, but—
STORE: Well, the point that we have to share with friends is that we don’t spend from the fund. We take an interest from the fund that comes into consideration in the budget. And there the research and science is, as any modern state, very important. You will find in in my country that a lot of research is going into energy, renewable, offshore wind, how we get CO2 out of gas and deposited through capture, major research undertaking. We are doing now major investment on Arctic affairs, Polar Year, the polar research year in 2032, which is going to mobilize all global polar research, will be led by Norway. And we are also putting government money into quantum research, together with private industry.

So, you know, we have to go where we have—not because we have a fund, but because we have science in our universities, in our research centers, and in our business. I was today with Kongsberg, Norwegian company, also present in Ottawa. And they are doing now software development, very impressive for somebody who cannot understand all the details, to how we protect our airports against drones in order to do the detection—
STUBB: Yeah, but you were late because of an airport problem today. (Laughter.) So we needed Kongsberg.
STORE: That was a U.S. airport problem.
No, so I agree with you. But, you know, I think there, again, each country has to go where it has, you know, comparative advantage. And we do.
STUBB: No one has asked us about our AI initiative yet. Just a hint. (Laughter.)
ZAKARIA: Want to get somebody at the back. I feel like there should be equal—yeah, the gentleman waving his hand. No, behind you, sir. Sorry.
Q: Sorry. Thank you, Fareed. Tom Nagorski with the _Cipher Brief_.
I want to come back to a question Fareed—
ZAKARIA: Can you keep the mic closer to you?
Q: A question Fareed asked earlier about—
ZAKARIA: We still can’t hear you. I think either you need a new mic, or—
Q: Can you hear me now?
ZAKARIA: Now we hear you.
Q: A question about Article 5, which Fareed asked about. I think it was you, President, who sounded very confident about President Trump’s commitment. Here at least, and I think Fareed’s question suggested that, it doesn’t seem at all clear. Can you say a bit more about why you are confident about the commitment from the United States right now? And are there plans within NATO for what happens if there is an incident and there is no response from the United States?
