And it’s quite possible that this will get worse because, I was just in Ukraine, and the industrial economy has essentially shut down because of the—because of what President Stubb was saying. The energy infrastructure has been damaged badly enough that very few factories, big factories, are running. Do you think Europe will be able to do what it takes to support Ukraine?
STORE: Well, part of that finance is becoming more and more Northern European. I think that the Northern Europeans have stood, you know, the course until now. I think that the way Ukraine is resisting is telling us the following, how do wars end? They end when the warring parties see that, you know, the war is not going to deliver what they went into this, and the pain of the war is going to exceed what you can benefit from the war. I sense that we are getting closer to that point, in the sense that it’s a war that obviously should have not started. Every purpose that was defined when it started has not been achieved, basically. And now we’re five years into it soon, and it should stop.
texts.2:
So I think, yes, it will be critical during this winter. But I think, you know, the Ukrainians have shown us again and again their will to resist this. They are not going to lay down. The Donbas scenario, where President Putin, you know, he wants Donbas. There are 200,000 people living there. And Ukraine controls this area. And they will not give it up. They cannot give it up. It will be against their constitution. And no Ukrainian leader can give up a territory with people that they have died for. So that will not happen. So, you know, does that mean that we will approach a moment—and I think the president and I have, you know, been old colleagues in in foreign policy for almost twenty years now. We see that that moment must approach.
And that’s why I think the U.S., although, you know, I regret that there is not financial support. I think, you know, that’s a mistake. But they are critically important to get the diplomacy moving. So we need focus, and we will spend some time this week, I think, to make that voice heard. You know, to have an American role in that diplomacy to get it going. And then it will be our responsibility to see to it that Europe, which will have to live with the aftermath of this conflict. This is a conflict in our territory. Russia is our neighbor. That we can define a security structure for the future. But that moment has to come sooner than later, that there is a start of the end of this war.
ZAKARIA: President Stubb, you are sometimes called a Trump whisperer for the Europeans. You do have a good personal relationship with him. You talk to the negotiators often. Do you get the sense that there is any real movement on the negotiation side? Again, when I was in Kyiv the feeling was they were being—they were being given the same old offers, that there was no real progress.
texts.3:
STUBB: Well, I think, Jonas and I were there, I think, a week before you. And I think the mood then was rather positive. And we had spoken to the American negotiators a few times before they went in and right after they came out. And we spoke to president Zelensky, was it a week ago, a week and a half ago in in Oslo, and we’ll see him here this week. I think the fact that Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff went to Moscow, that John Ratcliffe went to Moscow, that was significant. And then that the two negotiators went to Kyiv got the ball rolling.
Now, my feeling is that out of those early negotiations there’s now sentiment that the Anchorage deal is out of the window, so three plus two doesn’t exist anymore.
ZAKARIA: Just explain what that is.
STUBB: And that means that the Russians wanted to take three of the oblasts and leave two to the Ukrainians. And this was their sort of assumption of the deal in Alaska. And this is out of the window. As is Ukrainian neutrality. And I think they are going to get back to so-called trilateral negotiations—Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S.—on a lower level, trying to get perhaps a partial deal, which would have to do something with the Black Sea, with grain corridors, and energy corridors. So my sense is that things are moving. Does this mean that we’re going to get peace immediately? No. But there has to come a point when, you know, the Russians realize that enough is enough and they will not have achieved their goals, which was to basically take over Ukraine, deny its independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity.
texts.15:
ZAKARIA: Alex, you’ve been—President Stubb, you’ve been a serious scholar of international relations. You’re now a serious player. What is the most surprising thing that you found, going from being a scholar to a practitioner?
STUBB: Well, I always had this sort of E.H. Carr type of an idea, that I had a dream when I was young or came out of Furman University, my alma mater, in 1993, that I would be able to oscillate between the world of academia and the world of politics, or actually at the time civil service. Politics came quite late, in 2004. And I don’t think I’ve been surprised by anything except how much more I get out of taking time in one domain and coming back. So, for instance, I mean, I left politics permanently in in 2016. And I fully admit, I would not sit here had not, you know, Russia attacked Ukraine in 2022. I was always a NATO advocate, and then I was asked to run for president. And I thought, OK, I’ll do it.
But I had four years in academia, you know, writing my book and thinking about big concepts. And then coming back into a situation where you feel that you have curveballs coming at you every day at the pace of a fastball. And then to be able to conceptualize things and categorize things has helped me immensely. And the final point, I think in this job if you don’t read books and if you don’t write, you only get into this sort of churning process. And I think it would be very difficult for me to cope with it. So I just need to stop and do my reading, you know, either on a plane, or early morning, or whenever it is. So I’m just very fortunate that I’ve been able to go back and forth between academia and practice.
STORE: Can I say that I welcome him back to politics? (Laughter.) So—
ZAKARIA: And I hope you will share that advice to read with some other world leaders. (Laughter.)
STUBB: Oh, he reads a lot.
ZAKARIA: (Laughs.) Mike Froman.
Q: Well, first of all, thank you both for being here. Thank you, Fareed, for moderating this.
texts.16:
Mr. President, you mentioned the importance of middle powers. Mr. Prime Minister, you’ve just come from Canada, talking with Prime Minister Carney, the recent proponent of the role of middle powers. What, in reality, do you think the prospects and the limitations are for middle powers to play a central role in the world going forward, without the United States involvement or leadership?
STUBB: Well, I think Jonas and I don’t consider ourselves to be middle powers. Perhaps Norway, but not Finland. (Laughter.) No. So, you know, we talk about ourselves being in the back office. So if foreign policy is about values, interest, and power, we have values and interest. And the way in which we project power is through sharing information and being in the back office and helping out. But I would consider myself to be more of an institutionalist than a middle power kind of guy. I know we live in a middle power world, where you have these unholy coalitions and alliances coming up. And they, you know, have an impact. But I still believe that regional integration is the best way for a small country to work. Middle powers are probably not going to gain that much traction with the big powers, who want to only play the power game with the bigger countries. So China, the U.S., India. That’s why I think trying to get things into an institutional framework is probably more effective for small guys like us.
STORE: I agree with that. And then I think, you know, there’s a particular moment now where there is an opportunity for pragmatism. What can work? And where are there opportunities that you, without prestige, can go in and say, you know, if we put this together it may work. And here, I think, you know, again, like-minded countries—as I said, the president and I, we come from different parties, but I think we share this kind of.
STUBB: I’m independent. (Laughter.)
texts.17:
STORE: You were elected on the bill. (Laughter.) No, but the point here is that—and here and here I see also, you know, the Mark Carney appeal. I mean, he’s in in a very special situation with this—you know, this U.S. tension which is there. But it is also going after what can work in this world, where kind of the news is that more and more is not working. And that’s creating, you know, a certain also idea of potential optimism, that we can get things to work. On trade for example, we see that trade is breaking down in the sense that tariffs are coming in again. I think it is a very bad idea. It is hurting all parties. But 70 to 80 percent of world trade is still according to the rules.
So how do we work with WTO to reform it and make it, you know, sustain? How do we make the international cooperation that works and deliver results, make them vibrant? And here I think the Arctic, you know, it is an area of pragmatism that we look after. So here countries, like ours, and I wouldn’t call us middle powers either, but, you know, pragmatic countries that have open economies, highly digitalized. We don’t invent much AI, but we are probably the ones who use them most, and, you know, can spread it to a population where the level of education can take it on board. So we are active and engaged.
STUBB: Can I steal one of Jonas’ examples that he gave already, I think, when we were foreign minister way back in the Stone Ages. And it’s linked to middle powers. If you put the five Nordic countries together, we would be G-10. So that—you know, if we’re together, that kind of gives us a middle power status. And I think that’s very much in our DNA.
ZAKARIA: Ma’am, in the blue, yeah.
Q: Michelle Caruso-Cabrera, longtime journalist. Thanks so much for doing this.
texts.18:
Prime Minister, the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund does not invest in private equity, despite its large size. I’m sure that breaks the hearts of many people here in the audience. (Laughter.) Even as the number of publicly traded stocks in the world get smaller and smaller. Just this past week, the fund asked if it could invest in private equity, and yet the answer is no. Do you think that will ever change, and why is that?
STORE: Well, I think, you know, it is by nature, because it’s this kind of fund owned by—it’s a sovereign wealth owned by people. It has a certain risk averse. I wouldn’t exclude that that could not come, because it should look at the—at, you know, what you call the kind of universe of investment, needs to be countries where there where there is a rule of law for the equity markets and so on. It has evolved into investing in infrastructure, which is one big step. There was also a chapter where it invested in in real estate. So I wouldn’t exclude that coming. But, you know, there are quite high demands on control mechanisms, transparency, and how things can be available. But, you know, I wouldn’t exclude. But it’s not for the immediate.
ZAKARIA: Let’s take—follow the good example of the lady who just asked the question, and if you can direct your question to one of the two leaders, it’d be easier. So I think I saw back there. Yes, sir.
Q: Hi, my name is Hall Wang.
I’ll direct my question to the prime minister. So, on top of your country being really good at winning Winter Olympic medals, you’re also a great adopter of electric vehicles. As you know, the electric vehicle industry is becoming increasingly present with Chinese companies like BYD. Do you ever think it’s an intelligent, pragmatic approach to put tariffs on Chinese EVs to potentially protect Western car companies? And also, if you could share your preference for electric vehicles, that’d be fun as well.
texts.19:
STORE: Well, we were early in incentivizing electric vehicles. You know, taking away—we had VAT. And now the fact is that about 98 percent of new car sales in Norway is non-fossil. So that is a major achievement, and it’s helping us to get emissions down, and it is doing the right thing. The number of Chinese cars is going up. It’s up to Norwegians what they want to buy. I think we have a challenge when it comes to government, both local government and central government. Do you buy Russian—do you buy Chinese busses, for example? If you know that there may be intelligence gathering through the bus system, transport system? There are important questions to be asked. And probably the answer can be no.
And then, you know, Norway, we are not producing cars. But when I am in China, I second my European colleagues who say that, you know, there are reasons to challenge and question the way you support your industry, the way you subsidize it not through traditional subsidies but through a whole set of mechanisms very hard to penetrate. And this is building. This conflict is building. For a car-producing country like Germany, it is it is a very, very complex and dramatic issue. And I support European colleagues, you know, taking a firm line on that. I was foreign minister back at the time when China got into WTO. And we thought that was the right thing to do because we would have level playing field and rules to support. But then it has to work both ways. And here there are really, I think, issues that need to be handled.
ZAKARIA: Sir, over there on the aisle, exactly you.
Q: Hi. Jay Markowitz, Regeneron Ventures.
texts.20:
You each commented about playing the long game with ideas. And I would argue that the way to do that is by supporting science and scientists who do it. Now I think is an historic opportunity for other countries to step up and fill some of the gaps, become a more welcoming place and more supportive place to fund that research. I won’t pile on, on the $2.25 trillion opportunity that you have in Norway that you’ve mentioned. You’re investing in—you have invested in the stock market as well as infrastructure. But I’m curious what each of you think of this. You talk about the Nordic region together combined is like the G-10. So what are your thoughts about moving science forward and using that as a way to advance your growth? Thank you.
ZAKARIA: Alex, why don’t you start?
STUBB: Well, I mean, I think it’s the basis of everything. I mean, education is the basis of civilization, research and development and innovation is the basis of the economy. And, of course, right now from the U.S., unfortunately, there’s been a brain drain. And I think a lot of us in Europe are trying to work on, OK, how do we deal with this? I also believe that when it comes to R&D, it’s not only public money. I mean, Finland got out of the—a difficult situation, a banking crisis, in the early 1990s by putting a lot of public investment into R&D. But now when money is scarce, it needs to also come from the private side.
texts.21:
I’m actually extremely bullish about the Finnish economy at the moment, because we have a lot of the, you know, chokepoints or key elements of what it takes to be driven in an AI economy. You know, in terms of networks with Nokia, or in terms of quantum computing with e-companies, or in terms of a satellite industry. But that needs some kind of a cluster. So therefore, we have, for instance, what we call Aalto University in the Helsinki region, which has a lot of incubators and sort of mixes academia, science, and business. And I think this is sort of the interaction that you need in order for you to thrive. And, as an academic, I also think that, you know, it’s quite often in research a system of trial and error. So you try to work on something on a scientific method, and then you fail, and then you try again, and then you fail, and perhaps on a third time you come and get a solution. So this is a type of mentality that I’d like to see us have in Finland when it comes to research and development and education and learning.
ZAKARIA: Prime Minister, you must be asked all the time why don’t you spend your 2.25 trillion (dollars) on X, Y, and Z, but—
STORE: Well, the point that we have to share with friends is that we don’t spend from the fund. We take an interest from the fund that comes into consideration in the budget. And there the research and science is, as any modern state, very important. You will find in in my country that a lot of research is going into energy, renewable, offshore wind, how we get CO2 out of gas and deposited through capture, major research undertaking. We are doing now major investment on Arctic affairs, Polar Year, the polar research year in 2032, which is going to mobilize all global polar research, will be led by Norway. And we are also putting government money into quantum research, together with private industry.
texts.22:
So, you know, we have to go where we have—not because we have a fund, but because we have science in our universities, in our research centers, and in our business. I was today with Kongsberg, Norwegian company, also present in Ottawa. And they are doing now software development, very impressive for somebody who cannot understand all the details, to how we protect our airports against drones in order to do the detection—
STUBB: Yeah, but you were late because of an airport problem today. (Laughter.) So we needed Kongsberg.
STORE: That was a U.S. airport problem.
No, so I agree with you. But, you know, I think there, again, each country has to go where it has, you know, comparative advantage. And we do.
STUBB: No one has asked us about our AI initiative yet. Just a hint. (Laughter.)
ZAKARIA: Want to get somebody at the back. I feel like there should be equal—yeah, the gentleman waving his hand. No, behind you, sir. Sorry.
Q: Sorry. Thank you, Fareed. Tom Nagorski with the _Cipher Brief_.
I want to come back to a question Fareed—
ZAKARIA: Can you keep the mic closer to you?
Q: A question Fareed asked earlier about—
ZAKARIA: We still can’t hear you. I think either you need a new mic, or—
Q: Can you hear me now?
ZAKARIA: Now we hear you.
Q: A question about Article 5, which Fareed asked about. I think it was you, President, who sounded very confident about President Trump’s commitment. Here at least, and I think Fareed’s question suggested that, it doesn’t seem at all clear. Can you say a bit more about why you are confident about the commitment from the United States right now? And are there plans within NATO for what happens if there is an incident and there is no response from the United States?

Watched, not recruited? Orbán's alleged army informant reports
For years, Viktor Orbán, Hungary's prime minister for 16 years until May and Putin's most reliable ally in the EU, has said the communist secret police watched him but never recruited him. Now Hungary's last communist-era prime minister says he once held informant reports attributed to him.
Miklós Németh says the defense minister handed him three handwritten, signed reports in March 1990, shortly before Hungary's first free election. According to Németh, they described Orbán's fellow soldiers during his military service: their conduct, and their political, sexual, and religious orientation.
He couldn't verify who wrote them, though he believed he recognized Orbán's handwriting. He handed them back and kept no copies.
Years later, he was told the papers were with Géza Stefán, a KGB-trained head of Hungary's military security service. Stefán's files vanished from his safe the day after he died in 2009, and investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi wrote the alleged Orbán reports could have been among them.
Orbán says the communist authorities tried to recruit him and he refused. His spokesman called the claims "FAKE NEWS."

# Hungary's newly opened secret police archives revive questions about Orbán's communist-era past
Юстина Лісова  
Старша редакторка стрічки новин
06 November 2026 11:04
Newly opened Hungarian communist-era security archives have revived a decades-old controversy over whether former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán informed on fellow soldiers during his military service in the 1980s.
Investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyihas published a statement by Miklós Németh, Hungary's last communist-era prime minister, who claims he was shown three handwritten intelligence reports attributed to Orbán shortly before the country's first free parliamentary elections in 1990.
The reports allegedly described Orbán's fellow conscripts, including their behavior and political, religious and sexual views.
However, Németh acknowledged that he could not verify the authorship or authenticity of the handwriting and signatures. He returned the documents without making copies, and their current whereabouts are unknown.
Orbán has denied working as an informant, saying communist security services tried to recruit him during his military service but he refused.

# Hungary's newly opened secret police archives revive questions about Orbán's communist-era past
### What the archives show
On November 4, Hungary opened a public database of communist-era state security records as part of a broader effort by the country's new government to make historical intelligence files accessible.
A day earlier, Orbán published documents concerning himself and his wife, Anikó Lévai, on Facebook. He said the authorities had attempted to recruit him in the early 1980s and subsequently placed him, his wife and fellow opposition activists under surveillance.
According to Hungarian outlet Telex, an archival registration card identifies Orbán as a _társadalmi kapcsolat_, or "social contact," of military counterintelligence during his compulsory service.
Historians interviewed by Telex stressed that this designation did not mean someone was a formally recruited agent. Soldiers could be registered as contacts without signing cooperation agreements, and some were reportedly unaware of their classification.
Áron Nagy-Csere, a researcher at Hungary's Historical Archives of the State Security Services, told Telex that the archive holds no documents proving Orbán was recruited as an agent.

# Hungary's newly opened secret police archives revive questions about Orbán's communist-era past
### Alleged reports that disappeared
In a statement dated March 30, 2026, Németh recalled that then-Defense Minister Ferenc Kárpáti had shown him three original reports allegedly written and signed by Orbán.
According to Németh, Kárpáti later said the documents had passed into the possession of Géza Stefán, a former military counterintelligence officer trained by the Soviet KGB who subsequently headed Hungary's Military Security Office.
Panyi reported that sources interviewed for his book said a collection of compromising documents disappeared from Stefán's safe shortly after his death in 2009. It remains unclear whether the alleged Orbán reports were among them.
Németh submitted his written account and other historical materials to Hungary's state security archives this year. His statement has now been published with his permission.
Historian Krisztián Ungváry has questioned the reliability of Németh's account, arguing that it does not establish that Orbán was recruited or maintained a closer relationship with communist intelligence.
The allegations about Orbán's possible intelligence ties have circulated since 1989. His former political ally Lajos Simicska also raised questions about his past after the two fell out in 2015.
Panyi's investigation examines whether compromising intelligence material could have been used to influence Orbán, whose governments maintained close ties with Moscow and frequently clashed with European partners over support for Ukraine.
There is no verified evidence that Russia possesses such material or that Orbán's policies toward Russia or Ukraine have been influenced by alleged communist-era intelligence records.

# Hungary's newly opened secret police archives revive questions about Orbán's communist-era past
Юстина Лісова  
Старша редакторка стрічки новин
06 November 2026 11:04
Newly opened Hungarian communist-era security archives have revived a decades-old controversy over whether former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán informed on fellow soldiers during his military service in the 1980s.
Investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyihas published a statement by Miklós Németh, Hungary's last communist-era prime minister, who claims he was shown three handwritten intelligence reports attributed to Orbán shortly before the country's first free parliamentary elections in 1990.
The reports allegedly described Orbán's fellow conscripts, including their behavior and political, religious and sexual views.
However, Németh acknowledged that he could not verify the authorship or authenticity of the handwriting and signatures. He returned the documents without making copies, and their current whereabouts are unknown.
Orbán has denied working as an informant, saying communist security services tried to recruit him during his military service but he refused.
texts.6:
# Hungary's newly opened secret police archives revive questions about Orbán's communist-era past
### What the archives show
On November 4, Hungary opened a public database of communist-era state security records as part of a broader effort by the country's new government to make historical intelligence files accessible.
A day earlier, Orbán published documents concerning himself and his wife, Anikó Lévai, on Facebook. He said the authorities had attempted to recruit him in the early 1980s and subsequently placed him, his wife and fellow opposition activists under surveillance.
According to Hungarian outlet Telex, an archival registration card identifies Orbán as a _társadalmi kapcsolat_, or "social contact," of military counterintelligence during his compulsory service.
Historians interviewed by Telex stressed that this designation did not mean someone was a formally recruited agent. Soldiers could be registered as contacts without signing cooperation agreements, and some were reportedly unaware of their classification.
Áron Nagy-Csere, a researcher at Hungary's Historical Archives of the State Security Services, told Telex that the archive holds no documents proving Orbán was recruited as an agent.
texts.7:
# Hungary's newly opened secret police archives revive questions about Orbán's communist-era past
### Alleged reports that disappeared
In a statement dated March 30, 2026, Németh recalled that then-Defense Minister Ferenc Kárpáti had shown him three original reports allegedly written and signed by Orbán.
According to Németh, Kárpáti later said the documents had passed into the possession of Géza Stefán, a former military counterintelligence officer trained by the Soviet KGB who subsequently headed Hungary's Military Security Office.
Panyi reported that sources interviewed for his book said a collection of compromising documents disappeared from Stefán's safe shortly after his death in 2009. It remains unclear whether the alleged Orbán reports were among them.
Németh submitted his written account and other historical materials to Hungary's state security archives this year. His statement has now been published with his permission.
Historian Krisztián Ungváry has questioned the reliability of Németh's account, arguing that it does not establish that Orbán was recruited or maintained a closer relationship with communist intelligence.
The allegations about Orbán's possible intelligence ties have circulated since 1989. His former political ally Lajos Simicska also raised questions about his past after the two fell out in 2015.
Panyi's investigation examines whether compromising intelligence material could have been used to influence Orbán, whose governments maintained close ties with Moscow and frequently clashed with European partners over support for Ukraine.
There is no verified evidence that Russia possesses such material or that Orbán's policies toward Russia or Ukraine have been influenced by alleged communist-era intelligence records.

Watched, not recruited? Orbán's alleged army informant reports
For years, Viktor Orbán, Hungary's prime minister for 16 years until May and Putin's most reliable ally in the EU, has said the communist secret police watched him but never recruited him. Now Hungary's last communist-era prime minister says he once held informant reports attributed to him.
Miklós Németh says the defense minister handed him three handwritten, signed reports in March 1990, shortly before Hungary's first free election. According to Németh, they described Orbán's fellow soldiers during his military service: their conduct, and their political, sexual, and religious orientation.
He couldn't verify who wrote them, though he believed he recognized Orbán's handwriting. He handed them back and kept no copies.
Years later, he was told the papers were with Géza Stefán, a KGB-trained head of Hungary's military security service. Stefán's files vanished from his safe the day after he died in 2009, and investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi wrote the alleged Orbán reports could have been among them.
Orbán says the communist authorities tried to recruit him and he refused. His spokesman called the claims "FAKE NEWS."

# Bauman Named Big Ten Specialist of the Year
Carly Bauman (Michigan Photography)
Bauman Named Big Ten Specialist of the Year
3/21/2026 8:21:00 PM  | Women's Gymnastics
Share:
[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fmgoblue.com%2Fnews%2F2026%2F3%2F21%2Fwomens-gymnastics-bauman-named-big-ten-specialist-of-the-year&p[images][0]=%2Fimages%2F2026%2F3%2F21%2F20260321-gmw-bauman.jpg)
By: Megan McIntosh
**CHAMPAIGN, Ill.** -- Graduate student **Carly Bauman** of the University of Michigan women's gymnastics team was named the 2026 Big Ten Specialist of the Year on Saturday (March 21).
In just its second year as a conference award, Bauman joins Sage Kellerman of Michigan State as the only two recipients of the honor.
Bauman most recently earned her fourth Big Ten nod as she received her third first-team All-Big Ten honor and was a second team honoree in 2023. Bauman competed on three events in her sixth season and took home 10 individual event titles, including two on uneven bars, two on balance beam and six on floor exercise.
She notched Big Ten Specialist of the Week honors twice this season to bring her career total to five, while she recorded 14 scores of 9.900 or better -- including seven of her last eight routines on floor to close out the regular season. Bauman was named an AAI Award Finalist on Wednesday (March 18); she has also recorded a career-best 9.975 on all three of her events, including one time on floor in 2026.
_2027 Michigan women's gymnastics **season tickets** are now on sale. Single-meet tickets will go on sale Tuesday, Dec.8, at 9 a.m. ET. Join the ticket interest list to learn more about ticket options and to start planning your trips to Crisler to see the Wolverines!_

The Bloomingdale Police Department is honored to announce that we have received the AAA Gold Award for Community Traffic Safety for the third consecutive year. This prestigious award reflects our unwavering commitment to ensuring the safety of our roadways and the well-being of our community.
We are also proud to recognize Patrolman Kevin Peirsel and DPW Assistant Superintendent William Morris who received the Traffic Safety Heroes award for their exceptional contributions to traffic safety in Bloomingdale. Their dedication and hard work have been instrumental in achieving this recognition and in fostering a safer environment for all residents and visitors.
The department’s Traffic Bureau focuses on improving traffic and pedestrian safety, addressing residents’ concerns, and implementing measures to ensure safer streets within the community.
Chief Daniel Greenwood noted that this consistent recognition underscores the Bloomingdale Police Department’s unwavering commitment to public safety and its proactive efforts in fostering a secure environment for all residents and visitors. Together, we will continue to strive for excellence in all aspects of public safety.
In attendance were, Mayor D’Amato, Borough Administrator Sondermeyer, Chief Greenwood, Sgt. Zeidan, Ptl. Peirsel and DPW Assistant Superintendent Morris.

A powerful Pan-African icon, Sankara came to power in 1983 and led what became known as the Burkinabè Revolution, promoting anti-corruption, women’s liberation, environmental protection, and African self-reliance. However, his leadership was cut short on 15 October 1987, when he was assassinated during a coup led by his former ally Blaise Compaoré. Sankara and twelve companions were shot at the headquarters of the National Revolutionary Council in Ouagadougou. Compaoré ruled Burkina Faso for 27 years until he was removed from power during a popular uprising in 2014. In 2022, a military court sentenced him in absentia to life imprisonment for his role in Sankara’s assassination. Originally buried on the outskirts of Ouagadougou, Sankara’s remains and those of his companions were exhumed in 2015 for legal proceedings and later reburied at a memorial built at the site where they were killed. The government says honoring Sankara aims to preserve the revolutionary values and national pride he represented. # Bauman Named Big Ten Specialist of the Year
Carly Bauman (Michigan Photography)
Bauman Named Big Ten Specialist of the Year
3/21/2026 8:21:00 PM  | Women's Gymnastics
Share:
[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fmgoblue.com%2Fnews%2F2026%2F3%2F21%2Fwomens-gymnastics-bauman-named-big-ten-specialist-of-the-year&p[images][0]=%2Fimages%2F2026%2F3%2F21%2F20260321-gmw-bauman.jpg)
By: Megan McIntosh
**CHAMPAIGN, Ill.** -- Graduate student **Carly Bauman** of the University of Michigan women's gymnastics team was named the 2026 Big Ten Specialist of the Year on Saturday (March 21).
In just its second year as a conference award, Bauman joins Sage Kellerman of Michigan State as the only two recipients of the honor.
Bauman most recently earned her fourth Big Ten nod as she received her third first-team All-Big Ten honor and was a second team honoree in 2023. Bauman competed on three events in her sixth season and took home 10 individual event titles, including two on uneven bars, two on balance beam and six on floor exercise.
She notched Big Ten Specialist of the Week honors twice this season to bring her career total to five, while she recorded 14 scores of 9.900 or better -- including seven of her last eight routines on floor to close out the regular season. Bauman was named an AAI Award Finalist on Wednesday (March 18); she has also recorded a career-best 9.975 on all three of her events, including one time on floor in 2026.
_2027 Michigan women's gymnastics **season tickets** are now on sale. Single-meet tickets will go on sale Tuesday, Dec.8, at 9 a.m. ET. Join the ticket interest list to learn more about ticket options and to start planning your trips to Crisler to see the Wolverines!_

## Bloomingdale Police Department's Post
[December 3, 2024](https://www.facebook.com/BPDNJ/posts/pfbid02ms2rS1ZU46kSW4zuHBDs3wbGRneg4aM9kPy5rCQgiJS9JUYD8k7QaiXFnxJotZZ5l?__cft__[0]=AZgWM9ixULMjrF7X-f9aokV-kHm6Z4bBrh_GFqi75Y2JSdd--Y5isTLCq3hq-hJP1ZSi7xibsIu-AGcj87j-wkQmaIN8BPxMKmutD2_bUdx4h6dfRKH76gXln0trFA4MmDXiznqQQAKkVJvEK_Um5QXc0Gyv1Lo&__tn__=%2CO%2CP-R) ·
The Bloomingdale Police Department is honored to announce that we have received the AAA Gold Award for Community Traffic Safety for the third consecutive year. This prestigious award reflects our unwavering commitment to ensuring the safety of our roadways and the well-being of our community.
We are also proud to recognize Patrolman Kevin Peirsel and DPW Assistant Superintendent William Morris who received the Traffic Safety Heroes award for their exceptional contributions to traffic safety in Bloomingdale. Their dedication and hard work have been instrumental in achieving this recognition and in fostering a safer environment for all residents and visitors.
The department’s Traffic Bureau focuses on improving traffic and pedestrian safety, addressing residents’ concerns, and implementing measures to ensure safer streets within the community.
Chief Daniel Greenwood noted that this consistent recognition underscores the Bloomingdale Police Department’s unwavering commitment to public safety and its proactive efforts in fostering a secure environment for all residents and visitors. Together, we will continue to strive for excellence in all aspects of public safety.
In attendance were, Mayor D’Amato, Borough Administrator Sondermeyer, Chief Greenwood, Sgt. Zeidan, Ptl. Peirsel and DPW Assistant Superintendent Morris.

The title **Hero of the Soviet Union** (Russian:Герой Советского Союза,IPA:[[ɡʲɪˈroj sɐˈvʲetskəvə sɐˈjuzə]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Russian "Help:IPA/Russian")) was the highest distinction in the Soviet Union, awarded together with the Order of Lenin personally or collectively for heroic feats in service to the Soviet state and society.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-GSEncy-1) The title was awarded both to civilian and military persons.
The award was established on 16 April 1934, by the Central Executive Committee of the Soviet Union.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-sovietresolution-2) The first recipients of the title originally received only the Order of Lenin, the highest Soviet award, along with a certificate (грамота, _gramota_) describing the heroic deed from the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR. Because the Order of Lenin could be awarded for deeds not qualifying for the title of hero, and to distinguish heroes from other Order of Lenin holders, the Gold Star medal was introduced on 1 August 1939.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-sovietdecree1939-3) Earlier heroes were retroactively eligible for these items._[citation needed_]

A hero could be awarded the title again for a subsequent heroic feat with an additional Gold Star medal and certificate.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201215-4) The practice of awarding additional Orders of Lenin when the title was awarded multiple times was abolished by the Supreme Soviet of the USSR in 1988 during perestroika.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201215-4)
Forty-four foreign citizens were awarded the title.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-5)
The title was also awarded posthumously,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201217-6) though often without the actual Gold Star medal presented._[citation needed_]
The title could be revoked only by the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-7)
Most Soviet-bloc countries followed the Soviet example and instituted their own "Hero" awards. The Soviet-style "Hero" title is still used both in surviving current Communist states such as Cuba and in some non-Communist post-Soviet countries such as Russia, Ukraine, and others.
Individuals who received the award were entitled to special privileges, including:

*   A pension with survivor benefits in the event of the death of the title holder.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201214-8)  
*   Priority on the housing list with 50% rent reduction,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201214-8) tax exempt and an additional 45 square metres (480 sq ft) in living space.  
*   Annual round-trip[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201214-8) first class airline ticket  
*   Free local public transportation[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201214-8)  
*   Free annual visit to sanatorium or rest home[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201214-8)  
*   Medical benefits[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201214-8)  
*   Entertainment benefits[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201214-8)
Marshal Georgy Zhukov (center) wearing three Hero of the Soviet Union medals and Marshal Konstantin Rokossovsky (right) wearing two (1945)
Soldiers of the Red Army's 129th Rifle Division lift their comrades, awarded the title Hero of the Soviet Union, in celebration, 1943.

In total, during the existence of the USSR, the title of Hero of the Soviet Union was awarded to 12,777 people (excluding 72 stripped of the title for defamatory acts and 13 awards annulled as unwarranted), including 154 people who received the award twice (nine posthumously), three who received it three times, and two who received it four times. Among the Heroes of the Soviet Union, 44 people are citizens of foreign states. The great majority of them received it during World War II (11,635 Heroes of the Soviet Union, 101 twice Heroes, three thrice Heroes, and two four-time Heroes). Eighty-five people (28 posthumously) were awarded the title for actions related to the Soviet-Afghan War, which lasted from 1979 until 1989.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-9)
The first recipients of the award were the pilots Anatoly Liapidevsky (certificate number one), Sigizmund Levanevsky, Vasily Molokov, Mavriky Slepnyov, Nikolai Kamanin, Ivan Doronin, and Mikhail Vodopianov, who participated in the successful aerial search and rescue of the crew of the steamship _Cheliuskin_, which sank in Arctic waters, crushed by ice fields, on 13 February 1934. Valery Chkalov, who made the first-ever Trans-polar flight, was awarded the title on 24 July 1936. Valentina Grizodubova, a female pilot, was the first woman to become a Hero of the Soviet Union (2 November 1938)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-10) for her international women's record for a straight-line distance flight. Zoya Kosmodemyanskaya, a Soviet partisan, was the first woman to become a Hero of the Soviet Union during World War II (February 16, 1942), posthumously._[citation needed_]

According to Soviet war interpreter Elena Rzhevskaya, reports of several dead Hitler lookalikes in the days following his death stemmed from Colonel General Nikolai Berzarin's pledge to nominate the discoverer of Hitler's corpse for the award.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-Rzhevskaya-11) (Despite Soviet claims to the contrary, only Hitler's dental remains were ever certainly identified.)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-12)
Over 100 people received the award twice. A second Hero title, either Hero of the Soviet Union or Hero of Socialist Labour, entitled the recipient to have a bronze bust of their likeness with a commemorative inscription erected in their hometown.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-13)
Fighter pilots Aleksandr Pokryshkin and Ivan Kozhedub were three times Heroes of the Soviet Union.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201216-14) A third award entitled the recipient to have their bronze bust erected on a columnar pedestal in Moscow, near the Palace of the Soviets, but the palace was never completed.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChmelnizki2007286-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZubovich2020107-16)
After his release from serving a 20-year sentence in a Mexican prison for the assassination of Leon Trotsky, Ramón Mercader moved to the Soviet Union in 1961 and as Ramon Lopez[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-grave-17) was awarded the Order of Lenin and the Hero of the Soviet Union medal "for the special deed" by KGB head Alexander Shelepin._[citation needed_]

The only individuals to receive the title four times were Marshal Georgy Zhukov and Leonid Brezhnev. The original statute of the Hero of the Soviet Union, however, did not provide for a fourth title; its provisions allowed for a maximum of three awards regardless of later deeds. Both Zhukov and Brezhnev received their fourth titles under controversial circumstances. Namely, Zhukov was awarded a fourth title in direct violation of the statute.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201215-4) He was awarded the fourth time "for his large accomplishments" on the occasion of his 60th birthday on December 1, 1956. There is some speculation that Zhukov's fourth Hero medal was for his participation in the arrest of Lavrentiy Beria in 1953, but this was not entered in the records. Brezhnev's four awards further eroded the prestige of the award because they were all birthday gifts, on the occasions of his 60th, 70th, 72nd and 75th birthdays. Such practices halted in 1988 due to a decision of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR, which formally ended it._[citation needed_] By the 1970s, the award had been somewhat devalued. Important political and military persons had been awarded it on the occasions of their birthdays rather than for any immediate heroic activity._[citation needed_] All Soviet cosmonauts, starting from Yuri Gagarin, as well as foreign citizens from non-capitalist countries who participated in the Soviet space program as cosmonauts, received a Hero award for each flight, but no more than twice._[citation needed_]
Apart from individuals, the title was also awarded to twelve cities (Hero City) as well as the fortress of Brest (Hero-Fortress) for collective heroism during the War.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201214%E2%80%9315-18)

The last recipient of the title "Hero of the Soviet Union" was a Soviet diver, Captain of the 3rd rankLeonid Mikhailovich Solodkov on 24 December 1991 for his leadership and participation in a series of unprecedented extreme depth diving experiments.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-19) Following the collapse of the Soviet Union, this title was succeeded in Russia by the title "Hero of the Russian Federation", in Ukraine by "Hero of Ukraine" and in Belarus by "Hero of Belarus".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201217-6) Azerbaijan's successor order is that of National Hero of Azerbaijan and Armenia's own hero medal is that of National Hero of Armenia, both modeled on the Soviet one._[citation needed_]

Marshal Georgy Zhukov (center) wearing three Hero of the Soviet Union medals and Marshal Konstantin Rokossovsky (right) wearing two (1945)
Soldiers of the Red Army's 129th Rifle Division lift their comrades, awarded the title Hero of the Soviet Union, in celebration, 1943.
texts.3:
In total, during the existence of the USSR, the title of Hero of the Soviet Union was awarded to 12,777 people (excluding 72 stripped of the title for defamatory acts and 13 awards annulled as unwarranted), including 154 people who received the award twice (nine posthumously), three who received it three times, and two who received it four times. Among the Heroes of the Soviet Union, 44 people are citizens of foreign states. The great majority of them received it during World War II (11,635 Heroes of the Soviet Union, 101 twice Heroes, three thrice Heroes, and two four-time Heroes). Eighty-five people (28 posthumously) were awarded the title for actions related to the Soviet-Afghan War, which lasted from 1979 until 1989.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-9)
The first recipients of the award were the pilots Anatoly Liapidevsky (certificate number one), Sigizmund Levanevsky, Vasily Molokov, Mavriky Slepnyov, Nikolai Kamanin, Ivan Doronin, and Mikhail Vodopianov, who participated in the successful aerial search and rescue of the crew of the steamship _Cheliuskin_, which sank in Arctic waters, crushed by ice fields, on 13 February 1934. Valery Chkalov, who made the first-ever Trans-polar flight, was awarded the title on 24 July 1936. Valentina Grizodubova, a female pilot, was the first woman to become a Hero of the Soviet Union (2 November 1938)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-10) for her international women's record for a straight-line distance flight. Zoya Kosmodemyanskaya, a Soviet partisan, was the first woman to become a Hero of the Soviet Union during World War II (February 16, 1942), posthumously._[citation needed_]
texts.4:
According to Soviet war interpreter Elena Rzhevskaya, reports of several dead Hitler lookalikes in the days following his death stemmed from Colonel General Nikolai Berzarin's pledge to nominate the discoverer of Hitler's corpse for the award.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-Rzhevskaya-11) (Despite Soviet claims to the contrary, only Hitler's dental remains were ever certainly identified.)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-12)
Over 100 people received the award twice. A second Hero title, either Hero of the Soviet Union or Hero of Socialist Labour, entitled the recipient to have a bronze bust of their likeness with a commemorative inscription erected in their hometown.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-13)
Fighter pilots Aleksandr Pokryshkin and Ivan Kozhedub were three times Heroes of the Soviet Union.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201216-14) A third award entitled the recipient to have their bronze bust erected on a columnar pedestal in Moscow, near the Palace of the Soviets, but the palace was never completed.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChmelnizki2007286-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZubovich2020107-16)
After his release from serving a 20-year sentence in a Mexican prison for the assassination of Leon Trotsky, Ramón Mercader moved to the Soviet Union in 1961 and as Ramon Lopez[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-grave-17) was awarded the Order of Lenin and the Hero of the Soviet Union medal "for the special deed" by KGB head Alexander Shelepin._[citation needed_]
texts.5:
The only individuals to receive the title four times were Marshal Georgy Zhukov and Leonid Brezhnev. The original statute of the Hero of the Soviet Union, however, did not provide for a fourth title; its provisions allowed for a maximum of three awards regardless of later deeds. Both Zhukov and Brezhnev received their fourth titles under controversial circumstances. Namely, Zhukov was awarded a fourth title in direct violation of the statute.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201215-4) He was awarded the fourth time "for his large accomplishments" on the occasion of his 60th birthday on December 1, 1956. There is some speculation that Zhukov's fourth Hero medal was for his participation in the arrest of Lavrentiy Beria in 1953, but this was not entered in the records. Brezhnev's four awards further eroded the prestige of the award because they were all birthday gifts, on the occasions of his 60th, 70th, 72nd and 75th birthdays. Such practices halted in 1988 due to a decision of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR, which formally ended it._[citation needed_] By the 1970s, the award had been somewhat devalued. Important political and military persons had been awarded it on the occasions of their birthdays rather than for any immediate heroic activity._[citation needed_] All Soviet cosmonauts, starting from Yuri Gagarin, as well as foreign citizens from non-capitalist countries who participated in the Soviet space program as cosmonauts, received a Hero award for each flight, but no more than twice._[citation needed_]
Apart from individuals, the title was also awarded to twelve cities (Hero City) as well as the fortress of Brest (Hero-Fortress) for collective heroism during the War.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201214%E2%80%9315-18)
texts.6:
The last recipient of the title "Hero of the Soviet Union" was a Soviet diver, Captain of the 3rd rankLeonid Mikhailovich Solodkov on 24 December 1991 for his leadership and participation in a series of unprecedented extreme depth diving experiments.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-19) Following the collapse of the Soviet Union, this title was succeeded in Russia by the title "Hero of the Russian Federation", in Ukraine by "Hero of Ukraine" and in Belarus by "Hero of Belarus".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_of_the_Soviet_Union#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlander201217-6) Azerbaijan's successor order is that of National Hero of Azerbaijan and Armenia's own hero medal is that of National Hero of Armenia, both modeled on the Soviet one._[citation needed_]

In 2014, shortly before the Republic of Moldova signed its EU Association Agreement, nearly 99 per cent of Gagauzians voted in a referendum "to reject closer links with Europe in favour of joining the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union."[200] In 2015, "just over half of Gagauzians voted for the Russian-backed socialist candidate Irina Vlakh as governor."[200] Gagauzia continues to represent a serious challenge both to Moldova's territorial sovereignty and political stability due to Russia's systemic involvement in the region, especially by backing pro-Russian local parties and leadership candidates.[199][201] The European Centre for Minority Issues has also highlighted the role of supposedly neutral NGO groups in Gagauzia as a new front in Russia's hybrid-war against both Moldova and Ukraine.[199] The region's current local leader, Evghenia Guțul, in July 2023 thanked the fugitive Moldovan oligarch Ilan Shor, leader of the outlawed Moldovan pro-Russian opposition Șor Party, for his personal and financial support and his "willingness to do what it takes so that we may fulfil our election promises", and expressed a desire for deeper diplomatic ties with Russia.[202]

There is also substantial controversy over ethnic and linguistic identity in Moldova concerning whether the Moldovan language and Moldovan people constitute separate linguistic and ethnic groups to the Romanian language and Romanian people. The possibility of the unification of Moldova and Romania has remained a popular topic in both countries since Moldova's independence in 1991. Romania and Moldova enjoy exceptionally strong diplomatic relations. Romania supports Moldova's rapid accession to the European Union, provides vast economic assistance to Moldova's struggling economy, and provided up to 90% of Moldova's energy needs via discounted capped prices as Moldova sought to reduce its reliance on Russian oil and natural gas.[203][204] Relations have strengthened further since Russia's invasion of Ukraine.[205] Up to 74% of the Romanian public and more than 40% of the Moldovan public would support Moldova being integrated into Romania in one form or another, though most in either country believe that 'now is not the right time'.[206] A 2022 survey during the Russian invasion of Ukraine indicated that only 11% of Romania's population supports an immediate union, while over 42% think it is not the moment.[207]
Culture  
Main article: Culture of Moldova  
Mihai Eminescu, the national poet of Moldova and Romania  
Dimitrie Cantemir, Moldavian scholar of the early Enlightenment
Moldova's cultural tradition has been influenced primarily by the Romanian origins of its majority population, the roots of which go back to the second century AD, the period of Roman colonisation in Dacia.[208] Located geographically at the crossroads of Latin, Slavic and other cultures, Moldova has enriched its own culture adopting and maintaining traditions of neighbouring regions and of other influential sources.[209] The largest ethnic group, which had come to identify itself widely as "Moldovan" by the 14th century, contributed to the shaping of classical Romanian culture. The culture has been also influenced by the Byzantine culture, the neighbouring Magyar and Slavic populations, and later by the Ottoman Turks. A strong Western European influence in Moldovan literature and arts was prevalent in the 19th century. During the periods 1812–1917 and 1944–89, Moldovans were influenced by Russian and Soviet administrative control as well and by ethnic Russian immigration.[208]

Moldovans wearing national costumes in Chișinău
The country's cultural heritage was marked by numerous churches and monasteries built by the Moldavian ruler Stephen the Great in the 15th century, by the works of the later renaissance Metropolitans Varlaam and Dosoftei, and those of scholars such as Grigore Ureche, Miron Costin, Nicolae Milescu, Dimitrie Cantemir[g] and Ion Neculce. In the 19th century, Moldavians from the territories of the medieval Principality of Moldavia, divided into Bessarabia, Bukovina, and Western Moldavia (after 1859, Romania), made a significant contribution to the formation of the modern Romanian culture. Among these were many Bessarabians, such as Alexandru Donici, Alexandru Hâjdeu, Bogdan Petriceicu Hasdeu, Constantin Stamati, Constantin Stamati-Ciurea, Costache Negruzzi, Alecu Russo, Constantin Stere.
Mihai Eminescu, a late Romantic poet, and Ion Creangă, a writer, are the most influential Romanian language artists, considered national writers both in Romania and Moldova.[210]
Holidays  
Main article: Public holidays in Moldova
Most retail businesses close on New Year's Day and Independence Day, but remain open on all other holidays. Christmas is celebrated either on 7 January, the traditional date in Old Calendarists Eastern Orthodox Churches, or on 25 December, with both dates being recognised as public holidays.[211]
On 1 March features mărțișor gifting, which is a tradition that children and women wear a type of talisman that is given for good luck at the beginning of spring.[212]
Music  
Main article: Music of Moldova  
Zdob și Zdub performing at the 2011 Eurovision Song Contest
Among Moldova's most prominent composers are Gavriil Musicescu, Ștefan Neaga and Eugen Doga.

In the field of pop music, Moldova has produced the band O-Zone, who came to prominence in 2003, with their hit song "Dragostea Din Tei", which topped multiple notable single charts. Moldova has been participating in the Eurovision Song Contest since 2005. Another popular band from Moldova is Zdob și Zdub that represented the country in the 2005 Eurovision Song Contest, finishing sixth, also in 2021, with a similar result.
In May 2007, Natalia Barbu represented Moldova in Helsinki at the Eurovision Song Contest 2007 with her entry "Fight". Natalia squeezed into the final by a narrow margin. She took tenth place with 109 points. Then Zdob și Zdub again represented Moldova in the 2011 Eurovision Song Contest finishing 12th.
The band SunStroke Project with Olia Tira represented the country in the 2010 Eurovision Song Contest with their hit song "Run Away". Their performance gained international notoriety as an internet meme due to the pelvic thrusting and dancing of Sergey Stepanov, the band saxophonist. He has been dubbed "Epic Sax Guy". SunStroke Project featured again in the 2017 Eurovision entry "Hey Mama" which got third place.[213]
In 2015 a new musical project by the name of Carla's Dreams has risen in popularity around Moldova. Carla's Dreams reached the top charts in multiple countries in Europe with the release of their song "Sub Pielea Mea" in 2016. The song received a lot of airplay and reached number one place on the charts in Moldova as well as Russia. The group is still active and released their latest album in 2017. The theme of the musical group is "Anonymous" as they perform with painted faces, hoodies and sunglasses. The identity of the group members is still unknown.
Among most prominent classical musicians in Moldova are Maria Bieșu, one of the leading world's sopranos and the winner of the Japan International Competition; pianist Mark Zeltser, winner of the USSR National Competition, Long-Thibaud-Crespin Competition in Paris and Busoni Competition in Bolzano, Italy.
Media  
Main articles: Media of Moldova, Television in Moldova, Cinema of Moldova, and List of newspapers in Moldova

The right to freedom of speech and right to information are guaranteed by the Moldovan constitution. Reporters Without Borders improved Moldova's Press Freedom Index ranking to 28th in 2023 from 89th in 2020, partly due to government legal reforms which made it easier for journalists to access official information.[214][215] However, they cautioned that "Moldova's media are diverse but extremely polarised, like the country itself, which is marked by political instability and excessive influence by oligarchs." Moldova's media are divided into pro-Russian and pro-Western camps and on party political lines.[216] Oligarchs and political leaders strongly influence their editorial stances.
Television remains the most popular and trusted medium, while online social media is exerting increasing influence. Most private FM radio networks rebroadcast output from Russian and Romanian stations.[216] The first publicly funded national radio broadcaster, Radio Moldova, has been broadcasting since 1939 from the capital city, Chişinău. Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty is also widely available. Moldova's state-owned national radio-TV broadcaster is Teleradio-Moldova (TRM), which broadcasts the TV channel Moldova 1.
There were 3 million internet users by July 2022, approximately 76% of the population, and digital infrastructure is well-developed, with 98% 4G coverage of territory. There are a number of daily and weekly newspapers published in Moldova, among the most popular being Timpul de dimineață and Moldova Suverană, but print media has an overall small audience in Moldova. Independent media are struggling to ensure financial sustainability in the face of diminishing advertisement revenues due to inflation, economic stagnation and uncertainty caused by Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

In 2022, the government removed the broadcasting licenses from six television stations for broadcasting pro-Russian propaganda and disinformation about Russia's invasion of Ukraine in violation of the country's Audiovisual Services Code.[217] The government stated that this was done in order to "prevent the risk of disinformation or attempts to manipulate public opinion".[218] All six were either owned or affiliated with Ilan Șhor, a fugitive pro-Russian politician and businessman who fled to Israel in 2019 after being convicted of fraud and money-laundering and sentenced to 15 years in prison in absentia.[219] In October 2023 Orizont TV, ITV, Prime, Publika TV, Canal 2 and Canal 3 were also banned for undermining the local elections as well as blocking a number of Russian media outlets which includes the news agencies TASS and Interfax.[220]

The cinema of Moldova developed in the 1960s during the Soviet period, nurturing a small but lively film industry.[221] Following the collapse of the Soviet Union and Moldova's independence, the country's economic stagnation and poverty has hampered the Moldovan film industry.[221][222] Nevertheless, some films have seen some international success. Perhaps best-known are Lăutarii (1972), written and directed by Moldovan film-maker Emil Loteanu, and Wedding in Bessarabia (2009), which was co-produced by Romania, Moldova, and Luxembourg. In recent years Moldovan cinema has gained greater international attention. Carbon (2022), directed by Ion Borş, received positive acclaim by magazines such as Variety.[223] It was the winner of the Transilvania International Film Festival's Audience Award.[224] For the 37th edition of the Fribourg International Film Festival, Moldova was featured in its 'New Territory' section, which celebrates little-known film-making cultures.[225] In July 2022, the United Nations Development Programme announced that it would be using advanced equipment to transfer more than 1,600 films from the Moldova-Film archive for posterity and cultural preservation. The United States assisted by equipping in 2021 a digitisation laboratory to restore and preserve its archive feature and documentary films, representing an important part of Moldova's historical, cultural, and artistic heritage, and many of the films were broadcast on national TV with Romanian subtitles.[226][227]
Cuisine  
Main article: Moldovan cuisine
Moldova's fertile soil (chernozem) produces plentiful grapes, fruits, vegetables, grains, meat, and milk products, all of which have found their uses in the national cuisine. The fertile black soil combined with the use of traditional agricultural methods permits the growth of a wide range of foods in Moldova. Moldovan cuisine is similar to that of neighbouring Romania and Ukraine, and the regions share many traditional dishes, often with regional variations. Moldovan cuisine has historically been particularly influenced by elements of Russian, Turkish, and Ukrainian cuisine. Main dishes often include beef, pork, potatoes, cabbage, and a variety of cereals. Popular alcoholic beverages are divin (Moldovan brandy), beer, and wine—for which the country is known due to its high-quality offerings.[228][229]

Mămăligă
There are several traditional Moldovan dishes. Plăcinte are stuffed and deep-fried pastries with fillings such as soft cheese (often Urdă), cabbage, potatoes, apples, sour cherries and others, both sweet and savoury.[230] Sarmale is a typical Moldovan dish usually consisting of cabbage leaves stuffed with rice, peppers, carrots, meat, and baked in oil. Regional variations can also be found in other former parts of the Ottoman Empire. Mămăligă, a kind of porridge made from yellow maize flour, is another staple. It is popular in other countries as polenta and is often served with sheep's cheese and sour cream. Another traditional dish, plachyndy, is a kind of flatbread often made with kefir or buttermilk, wrapped around herbs, and pan-fried in oil.[231] Zeamă is a thin chicken soup, typically consisting of homemade chicken broth prepared with a smaller whole chicken, water, thin homemade egg noodles (tăiței de casă), and a variety of finely chopped vegetables and herbs.[232] Brynza is a soft sheep/goat cheese with a crumbly texture and tangy taste, mostly produced and popular in Slovakia, Romania, and Moldova, and often used in salads, pies, and dumplings.[233]
Borscht, a sour Eastern European soup made from beetroots, meat stock, and vegetables, is also popular and commonly served in Moldova. As with other parts of the region, pierogi (known as chiroște in Moldova) are another traditional staple and are often stuffed with a soft cheese in Moldova. The dough is made with wheat flour and is boiled in salted water, pan-fried in oil, or baked in the oven.[234][235] Medovik, a cake of Russian origin (and called Tort Smetanik in Moldova) is a popular layered cake with honey and smetana (sour cream) or condensed milk.[236]

Total recorded adult alcohol consumption is approximately evenly split between spirits, beer, and wine. Moldova has among the highest alcohol consumption per capita in world, at 15.2 litres (4.0 US gal) of pure alcohol imbibed in 2016.[237] This has fallen somewhat in recent years, but it remains a serious ongoing health concern.[238]
Sports  
Main article: Sport in Moldova  
Moldova national football team in 2015
Association football is the most popular team sport in Moldova. The governing body is the Moldovan Football Federation, which belongs to UEFA. The Moldova national football team played its first match in 1994, but never qualified to the UEFA European Championship. The most successful football club is Sheriff Tiraspol, the first and only Moldovan club to qualify for the group stage of the Champions League and the Europa League. Other winners of the Moldovan National Division include Zimbru Chișinău, Dacia Chișinău, FC Tiraspol and Milsami Orhei.
Trîntă (a form of wrestling) is the national sport in Moldova. Rugby union is popular as well. More than 10,000 supporters turn out for home internationals. Since 2004, playing numbers at all levels have more than doubled to 3,200. Despite the hardships and deprivations the national team are ranked 34th in the world.[239] The most prestigious cycling race is the Moldova President's Cup, which was first run in 2004. In chess, the Republic of Moldova has several international masters, among which can be mentioned Viorel Iordăchescu, Dmitry Svetushkin, and Viorel Bologan.
Radu Albot is one of the most successful Moldovan tennis players, with ATP singles (2019 Delray Beach Open) and doubles (2015 Istanbul Open) titles.

Athletes from Moldova have won European medals in athletics, biathlon, football, and gymnastics; world medals in archery, judo, swimming, and taekwondo; as well as Olympic medals in boxing, canoeing, shooting, weightlifting, and wrestling. Moldova made its Olympic debut at the 1994 Winter Olympics in Lillehammer. Olympic medalists include Sergei Mureiko, Oleg Moldovan, Vitalie Grușac, Veaceslav Gojan, and Serghei Tarnovschi. Nicolae Juravschi represented the Soviet Union at the 1988 Seoul Games, winning two medals.
